The house proceeded to consideration of a message from the senate insisting upon its amendment to Bill No. 97, to amend the Combines Investigation Act-Mr. Mackenzie King.

Combines Investigation Act

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the house will observe, the senate insists upon its amendment to Bill No. 07, an Act to Amend the Combines Investigation Act. By the bill as it went from this house to the senate it was sought to have the word "documents" dropped from the act as it stands, because the presence in the act of that word, in the opinion of the chief commissioner of the Trade and Industry Commission, renders the act useless. The opinion of the chief commissioner, Mr. Sedge-wick in that regard was supported, as was shown when I referred to the matter for the second time in this chamber, by the opinion of the Department of Justice. However, notwithstanding the views as expressed in that official way, supplemented by statements at some length as to reasons why the fears of the Senate would appear to be unwarranted, and the grounds upon which the amendment had been insisted upon not well founded, the senate insist upon their amendment. Of course the effect of the senate amendment, as I have already said, is that of rendering the Combines Investigation Act worthless.
May I point out that this is the third time this chamber has requested that the clause in question in the Combines Act should not include the word "documents" in order that the act might serve the purpose for which it was intended. At the last session the present leader of the Opposition (Mr. Bennett) then Prime Minister sought, this in a bill which passed this house and was sent to the senate, which bill contained a clause similar to the one which appears in the bill introduced by the present government. As the leader of the opposition has remarked, when the bill of last session returned from the senate it contained the amendment which the senate has now insisted should be made at this time. It was very late in the session and the government of that day permitted the senate amendment to remain, under protest.
At this session of parliament reasons were given in this house before the bill was sent to the Senate making clear wherein the amendment made by the Senate at the previous session rendered the Combines Investigation Act valueless. As a matter of fact it has not been thought advisable to proceed under the act since the Senate took their previous action. It will not be possible with t'he present suggested amendment to proceed under it, from now on, until the act is changed in the particulars indicated by this house.
For three times in succession within a year the Senate has refused in connection with the Combines Investigation Act to make a change which this house regards as imperative, and
has each time said so unanimously. May I point out that the last time we discussed the matter not only was the view of the government supported by the leader of the opposition but it was supported by the hon. member who leads the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. In short, the view of the government was supported by all hon. members. Ordinarily I assume the next step would be to ask for a conference between this house and the Senate. Indeed it was suggested before the bill was sent over to the Senate for the second time this session that a conference might be asked for. However, from a reading of the debate in the Senate it would appear that no useful purpose could possibly be served by a conference. The bill was sent back to the Senate last Saturday afternoon, and before the evening session the Senate had taken its action upon it. Apparently the opposition in that house did not seek even to ascertain the views which had been expressed in this house on the matter. In fact, reference to the debate of that chamber will show that when the leader of the government in the Senate was about to put the motion that the Senate do not insist upon its amendment, the leader of the opposition in the Senate anticipated what the leader of the government was about to say and suggested that the words in the motion should be that the Senate insisted upon its amendment. When the leader of the government in the Senate sought to have further consideration of the matter and drew attention to the fact that the Department of Justice had given an opinion on the matter, as well as Mr. Justice Sedgewick, who is Chief Commissioner of the Trade and Industry Commission and, who as hon. members well know, was for years an eminent judge of the High Court of Ontario, the leader of the government in the Senate was told by the leader of the opposition in that chamber that he was not aware of any will of the Department of Justice in the matter, that he had not seen any opinion of that department, and to put the matter briefly that he the leader of the opposition was not going to debate the matter over again. The leader of the opposition concluded by saying, "I intend to resist the position of the Commons, and to stand by the position the Senate has taken." I might also point out that another member of the opposition in the Senate stated that it might be well for the House of Commons to try the matter again next year.
In these circumstances I can not see that any useful purpose would be served by a conference at this time. As I said the other day, the government has determined to carry out certain investigations which i' regards as

Combines Investigation Act
very much in the public interest, and which it had intended to have proceeded with under the Combines Investigation Act. But seeing that the act has been rendered valueless by the action of the Senate we will, in all probability as I indicated the other day, where other provisions of the act respecting the trade and industry commission do not suffice proceed with these investigations under royal commission between now and the .time the house reassembles. The Combines Investigation Act will need to have several amendments. These amendments will be considered between now and, the next session of parliament, and the amendments which will be sent from this house to the senate at an early stage of the next session will include the clause which, as I have said, this house has three times already asked should be inserted in the combines act in order to render that measure effective. But, with the position what it is at the moment, I certainly do not intend as leader of this House of Commons or Prime Minister of this country to go on my hands and knees to the senate to ask for consideration at least of the representations which this house has made to the senate with regard to an act which is so all-important >to the public interest.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: I greatly deprecate the language the right hon. gentleman has just used. It is not seemly that the leader of the House of Commons should speak of one of the other houses, one of the three factors that constitute parliament, in the terms in which he has spoken. I think this is a case for the utilization of such conciliatory powers as we .possess, and our constitution has provided for a conference; that is the usual course. Why is a conference not held?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I gave the reason.

The reason being that the suggested amendment had been rejected by the senate. But there is another method, the method of conference, and twice to my certain knowledge we have been able through that method to arrange matters, because it afforded the opportunity for an understanding. I feel quite certain there has been a misunderstanding in connection with this matter, and that if the Minister of Justice and others were to meet the representatives of the senate there would be little or no difficulty in having it adjusted.
Neither is it correct to say that insistence by the senate upon the amendment in any sense nullifies the powers of the combines act.

It does not lessen them in the least; it has to do only with what may be done in a criminal court. There is no restriction upon the power of the commission under Mr. Sedge-wick to make any inquiries it may desire to make. The only result of the action taken by the senate is that thereafter there is a limitation upon the use that may be made of the material thus secured: the witness can set up the plea or defence that it will incriminate him, and that will be the end of it. Now the law will stand as it did before we introduced the amendment into this house. It does not take out the section that we passed last session; it leaves it as it then was. The proposal we made in this chamber was that-
No person shall be excused from attending and giving evidence and producing books, papers or records, in obedience to the order of the commission, on the ground that the oral evidence or documents required of him may tend to criminate him or subject him to any proceeding or penalty,-
That is one phase of it.
*-but no such oral evidence so given shall be used _ or receivable against such person in any criminal proceedings thereafter instituted against him, other than a prosecution for perjury in the giving of such evidence.
That is the section we sent from this house. The senate struck out the section and left the act just as it was. In other words, the action which we took dealing with documents was nullified by the action taken in the senate. I cannot but think that if the Minister of Justice were 10 discuss the matter with a committee of the senate in the sense in which it was done in this chamber last Saturday, the result would be an adjustment of the difficulties; because I still think the senate is labouring under a misapprehension with respect to what the action is, and is confusing two terms. Apparently, when the leader of the government in the senate pressed his motion the senate had not before it the discussion in this house, and I think, had the discussion in this house been before the senate, whom I know to be reasonable men, they would have taken a different attitude from that which they have now taken.
I cannot think it is conducive to the conduct of orderly government to suggest that any one house of parliament goes on its knees to any other house of parliament. That is entirely beside the question. They have coordinate powers and jurisdiction except with respect to money bills; they are a part of the constitution of this country. A method is provided by which reasons may be given when we disagree with them or they with us; they are read to the chamber affected, and then appropriate action is taken. I think it

Combines Investigation Act
would have been better to have a conference rather than to send the bill back the last time, because when there has been a rejection once of a suggestion of the commons the next appropriate course is a conference. I recall several occasions upon which a conference has been held with satisfactory results.

May I
ask my right hon. friend whether we had a conference last year on the same point?
No, because, as the hon. gentleman will remember, when it came down-

It was
the last day of the session.

It was a few hours
before the time fixed for prorogation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Have there
been conferences with this house this year on any other bills when the senate had rejected certain of their provisions?

Not that I know of.
That is why I say there should be a conference. Last year we had conferences; the year before we had conferences. Conferences are the method by which we meet together with the representatives of the other body and arrive at a conclusion, and I think it is the appropriate method; because in a debate in the house there is not the same opportunity for explanation and contact as there is when a conference is held. I cannot recall any conference I have known of that has not resulted in a satisfactory adjustment. I feel that if a conference were held there would be no necessity for using the language that has been used, nor would there be any cause for complaint or any grievance against another chamber. That is the position I desire to make clear. I think the senate is entirely in error in rejecting the proposals we have made in the measure we passed. I think so for the reason. I gave in the house the other day, and I will not repeat it. I also feel confident, from my knowledge of the members of the senate as reasonable men, that if they understood clearly the effect of our proposal they would not so summarily reject it. Further I believe that a conference of a few minutes' duration. would remove the difficulties, and I think we are not taking the right course in not holding one. It is no lessening of our own dignity or our own authority or importance to deal with the senate in. a manner which heretofore has always been the method employed when there has been a deadlock. I regret very much that the minister has taken the view that the conference should
not be held. It is not conducive to harmonious working, nor in the long run will it improve the position of the institution of parliament in this country.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The right hon leader of the opposition says be thinks f conference should have taken place at th< present stage.
After the first rejection.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: After the first rejection. May I point out that the senate has rejected several clauses of bills which have been sent over from this house in the course of this session, and in no instance has anyone suggested that a conference should take place at that stage; indeed a conference was not necessary, because the senate at the time was prepared to reconsider its attitude, and on reconsidering it they did accept in most cases the views of the House of Commons. There is no reason why a conference should have taken place after the first reading in the case of the combines bill any more than it should have with respect to the harbours bill and several other important bills-

Oh, yes; because last
year they rejected it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
-which have gone over from this house. That is the first point. In the second place, may I say my right hon. friend is wrong when he says that the reason we are not asking at the moment for a conference is that the senate insists upon this amendment. That is not the reason. If the senate had taken due notice of what was said in this house, if it had taken notice of what the leader of the government in the senate asked its members to consider, namely the opinion of the justice department, the opinion of Mr. Sedgewick, and I may add, the opinion of the right hon. leader of the opposition, and the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Confederation (Mr. Woodsworth), and if there had been a disposition to consider the matter at all, I think then that possibly a conference might have served some useful purpose. May I point out again just how all-important the request of this house is and why the attitude of the senate at this time would seem to render any conference fruitless. The Honourable Mr. Sedgewick has given in a sentence or two his opinion as to the significance of the clause in the amended form in which this house wishes to have it appear:
The purpose of the amendment is not to render admissible documents otherwise inadmissible, but to provide that admissible docu ments are not inadmissible.

Combines Investigation Act
If the section stands, the best thing that could happen to a person guilty of combining in restraint of trade is to be required on investigation to produce the documents proving the offence. Thereafter he will be immune from conviction by means of the agreement.
Did the leader of the government in the senate bring that opinion and the opinion of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) to the attention of the senate?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
As my hon. friend has asked me that question, I will answer it by reading from the senate report. It is as follows:
Hon. Mr. Dandurand: 

that the Senate do not insist upon its amendment. I suppose my Right Honourable friend after having made a noble fight to affirm his own principles, will abide by the will of the Department of Justice, supported by the opinion of Mr. Justice Sedgewick, and will vote for my motion.
Mr. Sedgewick's opinion is referred to there specifically.
Did he read it?
It was not read.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It was not read, but for what reason? Immediately after the leader of the government used those words in the senate, the right hon. leader of the opposition in the senate used these words:
I do not know of any will of the Department of Justice in parliamentary matters, and I have not seen any opinion of the Department of Justice.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Listen to what follows:
To put it briefly-for I am certainly not going to debate the matter over again-I intend to resist the position of the Commons and to stand by the decision the Senate has taken.
What further opportunity was offered to the leader of the government in the senate to discuss the matter at that stage?

He should have seen
the two opinions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The right hon. leader of the opposition says that the senate action does not render the act ineffective, that other provisions of the act remain, but the other provisions are not as important as this one. Mr. Sedgwick says that this provision is all-important; that if it is not there you simply enable a man. who has taken a course of proceedings which may be criminal to protect himself against any subsequent criminal proceedings by attempting 
to proceed under the Combines Investigation Act. I am reminded that Mr. Sedgewick's views were expressed in the discussion which took place when we first dealt with the matter on June 12.
But it was a subsequent opinion which was read later.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The first opinion covered the essential points. It was after this that the leader of the opposition in the senate stated that he did	not	see any object	indebating the question further. In these circumstances there would	appear to	be	no
prospect of having the amendment made at this time. Having regard for the language used by the leader of the opposition in the senate I certainly think it would be quite futile to attempt anything further by a conference.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are apparently unanimous in	our	opposition	to	thesenate amendment.	We	differ only as	to
method. While I should be the very last to advise going on our knees to the senate, it does occur to me that since a conference is the recognized procedure, it might be a good thing to go through every possible step, if for no other reason than to pile up a case against the senate and leave them no loophole whatever. I say to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) that I am very glad indeed that the government has determined to go through with the inquiry in spite of the senate.
I should like to take this occasion to suggest to the government that the people generally-I hope I can interpret aright their ideas-are ready for the government to take sonm steps to curb the power of the senate in .this country. As every hon. member knows, in Gieat Britain the House of Lords, to which in its functions our upper house to a certain extent corresponds, is unable to thwart permanently the will of the people. As I understand it, they can twice reject legislation passed by the commons, but when such legislation is presented a third time it must go through automatically. In any case the House of Commons in England has a club over the House of Lords in that it can create a larger number of lords. I think we have the most antiquated form of control by a second chamber to be found in any democracy. Since the Liberal party has for years urged the reform of the senate, in view of the various incidents that have recently taken place it is high time steps were taken to reform the senate, if necessary by changes in our constitution.

Dismissals-Mr. Bennett
In this particular case the situation is aggravated by the fact, known to all, that a well known member of the senate was recently involved in an inquiry. It is an outrage that the fullest inquiry into what is a very serious state of affairs should be blocked by a chamber which has not taken action against certain of its members.

May I draw
attention to the fact that the opinion of Mr. Sedgewick was brought to the attention of the senate on June 17, 1936.

That was the first
opinion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes, and it
includes the following words in conclusion:
I am quite satisfied in my own mind that the Dominion Trade and Industry Commission *-of which I am chief commissioner-would not risk having an investigator require the production of any documents until this act is amended.
I hope it may not be considered presumption on my part to say the amendment suggested is indispensable to a proper administration of the Combines Investigation Act.
Apparently the fact that Mr. Sedgewick's opinion had been cited in this house, and that Mr. Sedgewick had ventured an opinion was resented by the leader of the opposition in the senate instead of inducing further consideration, because I find the following words on page 579 of the senate record:
Right Hon. Mr. Meighen:	Yes.	_
Honourable members, I want to make a brief comment on the letter of Mr. Justice Sedgewick, just read by the leader of the government. The intimation of the letter is that the amendment made in this house and accepted by the other house, was merely in the nature of a last gasping spasm while we were in the midst of death.
As far as this house is concerned, it was nothing of the kind.
So far as this house is concerned, there will not be any last gapping spasm in connection with securing further action in this matter from the leader of the opposition in the senate. I want to say to my hon. friend who has just spoken (Mr. Woodsworth) that I concur very strongly in the views he has expressed on these matters which so vitally affect the well being of the great masses of the people of this country. Where the House of Commons, representing the people in their elected chamber stresses at least on three occasions the necessity for some all important legislation, unless there is something in the nature of very exceptional reasons to the contrary, that legislation should be granted by the senate.
I would say further that this is not the only piece of legislation which the present government has introduced at t'his session,
which we regarded as of importance in dealing with the most difficult of all problems facing the country at the present time, and which the senate has thrown out. It may be just as well for hon. members of the Senate to have a month or two to reflect upon what is going to be the consequence of repeated action of this kind; and, believing that reflection is advisable, the government proposes to allow the matter to stand as it is for the present, with respect to the Combines Investigation Act, but to proceed again at an early stage next session with amendments to that measure including the one which we have endeavoured to have carried at the present session.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: For the purpose of setting the facts right, and in answer to my hon. friend from St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan), I may say that not only was the opinion of Mr. Sedgewick given to the senate on June 18, when this bill was in committee of the whole in the senate, but the opinion of the Department of Justice was also given to the members.
Not the second opinion.

I have no doubt the first opinions were before the senate, but the second opinions were not. I should have had great confidence in the conciliatory presentation of the case by the Minister of Justice to the members of the senate. In the last five years I have been on joint committees of the house and the senate and I believe that on one of them the present Minister of Justice was also a member. In any case, a reasonable presentation by oral argument, in which misapprehensions are removed, will almost certainly lead to an amicable agreement with respect to almost any difference of this kind.
Amendment read the first time.

maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT WITH RESPECT TO DISMISSALS

speechtext: Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee of supply.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT WITH RESPECT TO DISMISSALS
speechtext:
This would seem to be the only appropriate opportunity that will be afforded this session to present grievances before supply is granted, and I desire to direct attention, in no acrimonious spirit, to one or two matters that have arisen out of the conduct of government in connection with appointments to the public service and dismissals. I am not for a moment dealing with that phase of administrative action that has to do with ordinary employment and dismissals. I
Dismissals-Mr. Bennett

recognize, as I have so frequently said, that the government of the day must necessarily, under our institutions, give effect to the views of its supporters and make appointments and dismissals of those who are not protected by the terms of the Civil Service Act or who have in other ways, by other methods, made themselves amenable to the punitive provisions of our statutes with respect to those who are in the public service. But there is another phase of the matter to which I should like to direct attention. It is far more important in one sense to every member of this house than any mere question of patronage because it affects an arrangement that was made many years ago and which in the main has successfully worked, but one that can work only with the exercise of the utmost good faith on the part of those who are responsible for its administration.
In 1911, when Sir Robert Borden came into office, a discussion took place in the first session regarding the question of patronage and dismissals from the public service. Sir Robert Borden said:
I would like to point out to my hon. friend what he seems to have forgotten, that with respect to both the inside service and the outside service this matter has been settled. In the first place by a statute of Canada concerning the inside service, in the second place by a resolution of this house, concurred in by both political parties with regard to the outside service. So far as the inside service is concerned, the statutory provision to which I desire to call attention is to be found in the act of 1908 introduced and passed by the late administration. Section 43 of that statute is as follows:
No officer, clerk or employee in the civil service shall be debarred from voting at any dominion or provincial election if under the laws governing the said election he has the right to vote; but no such officer, clerk or employee shall engage in partisan work in connection with said election.
That has been somewhat modified, amended by section 55 of the Civil Service Act; but the general purpose is exactly the same and the end sought is attained, I think, by the use of substantially similar words. Sir Robert Borden continued:
Now, so far as the outside service is concerned, the rule was embodied in a resolution of the House of Commons moved by Mr. Lake on the 17th July, 1905, and accepted by my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) who was then leading the government, and that rule is in these words:
That whilst it is desirable that every official in the employ of the government of Canada, should enjoy perfect freedom of political opinion, and the untrammelled exercise of his franchise in accord therewith, no official should be engaged, or permitted to engage, in partisan work of any description in the election of a representative to the provincial or dominion legislature.

On the same page-890-referring to Mr. A. K. Maclean, he said:
Now, my hon. friend has spoken of what should be necessary to convince the government or a minister of the crown that an official has taken an offensive part in any election. There are obviously some cases in which inquiry would be rather futile. For example, on the 21st of September last, I myself personally saw three office-holders of this country engaged in active partisan work in the city of Halifax. ... In that ease I would not grant an inquiry because I saw it with my own eyes.
At page 891, he said:
Now, my hon. friend is anxious that inquiry should be had in proper cases, and so am I. No one is more unwilling to dismiss officials that I am, but where the government or responsible ministers is convinced that an official has been guilty of violation of the plain terms of a statute or of a resolution of the House of Commons concurred in by both political parties, by which his conduct ought to be guided. I would ask my hon. friend what alternative would a government have in a case of that kind?
Then Mr. E. M. Macdonald, member for Pietou at that time, raised a very interesting question as to whether or not representations made by a defeated candidate would have the same force and effect as those made by a member, and he put the case very shortly in these words, as reported at page 923:
I' have no objection to an offensive partisan being dismissed, but we should have evidence to bear out the charge that lie is an offensive partisan. I am not here to say that a statement made by a member of this house under his hand in writing to the minister giving specific facts would not be sufficient evidence. I think that every member of this house is entitled to be considered as worthy of credence and there is this further protection that we can discuss the question in the house with the member who makes the statement. But when we come to deal with the written statement of a defeated candidate-
Mr. Rhodes: Does the hon. gentleman object to a minister taking the Recommendations of a defeated candidate?
Mr. Macdonald: Most certainly, and I have just given the reason why. We are now dealing with the question of the minister being satisfied by the evidence that a certain fact is true and the minister must justify his judgment to parliament. If he takes the statement of a member of parliament, that statement can be discussed in this house in the presence of the member who made it.
But if he takes the statement of a defeated candidate, he takes the statement of one who cannot discuss the question here, who cannot even give the details to the minister, or put them on record in the department as well as one can who holds a place in this house.
In 1928, on May 29, the then member for St. Lawrence-St. George brought to the attention of the house a case in- which a gentleman had been dismissed for partisanship. He had held office for seven years and seven months and was efficient. An inquiry was asked for

Dismissals-Mr. Bennett
but not granted. It was contended that as the minister had given a certificate he should be dismissed without further inquiry. The present Minister of Trade and Commerce in that debate said, at page 3526:
I will admit that the matter to which the hon. member has just referred has given me some little concern. The dismissal took place entirely in accordance with the principle that has been observed by all parties. . The complaint of a member of the house that an individual has been exercising partisanship in elections has always been accepted by the minister as a reason for dismissal. I have followed that principle, but I am glad to say there have not been many instances in my own department. I am not going to express an opinion as to whether that is a good practice to follow, although perhaps I might be just so bold as to say that I have a good deal of sympathy with the position taken by my hon. friend. Although many members may differ with me, I can see no particular reason why, where a man happens to be in the service of the government, he should not be allowed to exercise any influence he may have on behalf of any political principle in which he believes. However, I will have to take any responsibility there may be in following out the practice that has always been followed.
The result was that the gentleman dismissed from office was without any appropriate remedy. I am going to refer to that presently. During the progress of the first debate, to which I have alluded, Sir Wilfrid Laurier was not entirely in accord with what had been said by the previous speaker. Sir Wilfrid said:
I beg my hon. friend's pardon. We said in 1896 that no man should be dismissed unless he was first given the opportunity of being heard. But I said also that we would accept the written statement of a member of parliament, giving the facts, and asking for the dismissal. That is the rule we laid down, and we have lived up to it. I am told by hon. gentlemen opposite that we did not live up to that rule. I do not admit the charge. I think we did, but even if we were deficient I would expect that the hon. gentlemen who are on the treasury benches at present would at least act according to their own doctrine. Are they going to throw over their own doctrine and institute dismissals right and left without giving any man the opportunity of defending himself or without any member of parliament taking the responsibility of placing on record a charge against the man whose dismissal he seeks?
He then proceeds, and these words are important:
I would insist on the leader of the government that he should enforce the rule that no man should be deprived of office without being given the opportunity of defending himself or at least unless the member of parliament who asks for his dismissal has the courage to put on record the reasons why he demands it.
That principle was the one to which I alluded as being under discussion by the Prime Minister, Sir Robert Borden, in 1911-12.
Then we come to 1923, and according to Hansard for February 15, 1923, at page 286, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) used these words:
In some cases charges have been preferred against certain officials by hon. members of this house. Where an hon. member has been prepared to state to the house that of his own knowledge an offence contravening the provisions of the Civil Service Act respecting political partisanship has been committed, the government has acted under the provisions of the Civil Service Act, which provide that a civil servant guilty of political partisanship shall not be retained in the service. I think that list will cover any of the dismissals to which my right hon. friend has referred.
Mr. Meighen: I presume that that list would cover practically every case, because the statement from any member that a man has been guilty of political partisanship is not very hard to secure from a partisan supporter.
To which Mr. Mackenzie King replied:
I did not say a statement from any member. I said a statement from an hon. member of this house that of his own knowledge a civil servant had been guilty of a certain offence which was in the opinion of the government sufficient to warrant his dismissal under the provisions of the Civil Service Act.
That principle having been accepted, I am rising in my place this morning for the purpose of directing attention to the fact that it is based upon one assumption, which is that an hon. member of this house who certifies to such a condition has satisfied himself of his own personal knowledge as to the authenticity of the statements which he makes and that they are true. But if he sees fit to make a statement without regard to the fine detail of its being true or untrue and the man is dismissed, I think probably the man has an action against that member of parliament because he has compassed his dismissal and destroyed his position. At any rate I think the question will be determined in some of the courts of the country within the next year, because there are cases in which members of this house have certified that a man has been a partisan, of their personal knowledge, when as a matter of fact not only was the man not a partisan but he took no part in the elections in any way. But he has lost his position, with all the rights that appertain to it and obviously, having suffered damage, that matter will have to be contested in some other way.
The cases to which the hon. member for St. Lawrenee-St. George referred in a previous parliament need not now be discussed, but there are three cases to which I desire to direct attention because they affect this matter very directly. Some years ago a man

Dismissals-Mr. Bennett

who occupied a position on an Indian reserve was dismissed from office on the certificate of the member of parliament for the district in which he lived. The servant of the Indian department said the member had been incorrectly informed, that the member had no knowledge of him personally and did not know him at all. In the end, after much effort, (the unfortunate man having been out of office for years, an investigation was obtained. The investigation was held and the secretary of the Liberal association in that community was called as a witness. Without a single dissenting voice they all agreed that this man had taken no part in the elections and that they had seen no evidence of his activity in any shape, form, kind or description whatever. That man lost his position by an improper certificate having been given by a member of parliament.
Since the present government came into office several cases have occurred in which, under the certificate of members of parliament, employees 'have been dismissed. Those returns have been tabled in this house during this session, but there are two cases in Quebec to which particular attention is directed because the papers brought down in the house indicate that a very grievous wrong has been done to an unfortunate man. One is the father of eight children and he has been in the employ of the government for a very long time, in fact since November, 1915, twenty-one years this fall. No complaint has ever been made against him, but in a letter directed to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin) on the 29th January, 1936, a member of parliament stated that to his personal knowledge this man was guilty of political partisanship. Immediately the man was removed from office. As soon as he ascertained why he had been removed he began to gather together his friends, who were all able to say that for twenty-one years he had taken no part in politics, realizing how important it was for him to make a living for himself and his eight children. He has supported that statement further by a statutory declaration which he made on the 19th day of March, 1936. In that declaration he makes the following statements :
I,	the undersigned, Michel Bedard, of Bois-chatel, do declare and say:-
1.	I was employed by the public works department of Ottawa, as chauffeur, at the Quebec post office building, since the 28th of November, 1915;
2.	Since then, I have always worked for the same department in the same capacity, and my work was always satisfactory to the department;
3.	During the time I have been employed by the Department of Public Works, as above

mentioned, I never did any political partisanship; 1 never took any interest in the political campaigns and all what I did was to vote, according to my own conscience;
I have never taken any part in any meeting or any political discussion;
4.	I am the father of eight children and, since I have been dismissed by the department, I am without work, and I cannot see where I can find some;
5.	No complaint was ever made before against me, and I do declare that I do not deserve the situation in which Mr. Wilfrid Lacroix put me lately in asking my dismissal as he did;
6.	It is absolutely impossible that Mr. Wilfrid
Lacroix be aware of any act of political partisanship on my behalf, I never met him anywhere and I believe that he does not even know me personally;	_
7.	I make this solemn declaration according to the federal statutes, to have the same effect as if it was a declaration duly sworn.
. And I have signed:
(Signed) Michel Bedard. Solemnly declared before me,
this 19th day of March, 1936.
(Signed) F. O. Demin,
Commissioner Superior Court,
Dist. of Quebec.
The reason I am directing this matter to the attention of the house to-day is that I have not seen any evidence on the part of my fellow members, even though they are supporting the government in large numbers, that would induce me to believe they would consciously do an injustice to a man who has been in the employ of the government for twenty-one years. I have no reason to believe that the Prime Minister would desire that that be done. The effect of this is to throw a man on the street after twenty-one years of service in a particular position. The file is here, having been brought down in consequence of a motion passed by the house, and the file indicates clearly that the Minister of Public Works acted upon representations made to him by a member of parliament. The member of parliament asked that it be done, the Minister of Public Works therefore did it. I am not complaining of the Minister of Public Works having done it, but I am saying that it creates an almost intolerable position if the government is not prepared to take steps to protect one who has thus been injured, thus been deprived of his position. I said a moment ago that I believe the man who made the recommendation has subjected himself to an action. I have not much doubt about that, although it may be that as a member of parliament he can protect himself.
The other man was employed from October 8, 1930, and the man who was appointed to office believed that the first man, who has made a declaration in the same sense, had obtained a position to which he was entitled.

Dismissals-Mr. Bennett
But the report made indicates that that was incorrect, and the people of the settlement in which the man lives, without regard to their political faith, signed a recommendation to Mr. Lacroix, M.P., asking that the injury which had been done to this other man, namely Mr. Ubald Vezina of Beauport, be undone. He makes a declaration, which I shall not take the time to read, in exactly the same sense as Mr. Bedard. He says he has not been interested in political matters, nor has he been a partisan since his appointment, but he has lost his job because a member of parliament made a certificate upon which the Minister of Marine took the steps I have indicated, and he was replaced by another.
These two cases I mention. There are two or three others, which perhaps I should not deal with at length at this time of the session, but I desire to invite the attention of the government and the house to the principle involved. It is of far-reaching consequence, and I believe that appropriate measures should be taken to place in the estimates provision for this man. That is a strong statement, but if a man who denies any partisanship has been deprived of his position on that ground, I suggest he should be allowed an investigation. I ask the government to provide an investigation for these men, either before a judicial commission or by such other commission as they think proper. In other words, in view of the challenge to the statement made by the member of parliament, should he not now have the right to present his case before a proper tribunal?

maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT WITH RESPECT TO DISMISSALS
speechtext:
I should say the second one would be regarded as not a permanent employee, although I cannot say with certainty. The record is not clear on it and I therefore speak subject to correction on that point. But even if he were a temporary 12739-257J
employee I suggest to the government the desirability of following the case and permitting an investigation.
If hon. members take the trouble to look through the records of the last five years they will find that in some cases complaints were made that we set up too many investigations. Well, Mr. Speaker, I hold the view that it is better to suffer from giving men a chance to be heard, as Sir Wilfrid Laurier contended, than to take arbitrary action if there is a possibility of being wrong. Mr. Macdonald, of Pictou, who presented the case in 1911 or 1912, felt that there was an obligation upon a member of parliament whose honour was pledged by reason of a certificate he gave, but one ventured to point out that in these days of extreme partisanship you might have a situation which would be difficult to reconcile with that principle.
I do not desire to make any acrimonious observations with respect to the matter:	I
still believe in the fairness of mind of the Canadian people, regardless of what party may be in power. I hope that steps will be taken to afford to these men the right of investigation, and that if it is found, as was found in one case, that they have been improperly removed, it will be seen that they are recompensed for what has happened. In the case of this unfortunate man who was in the Indian department, it was years later when he got the investigation, because, he having been dismissed before the late government took office, they felt hesitant about granting an investigation. But finally the minister of the department said: This man has pleaded with me for his own reputation. He said: "My reputation is at stake. I accepted office and pledged myself by that acceptance that I would not engage in political activities, and I have kept faith in that regard." That was in 1927. Finally a commission was appointed and after hearing the evidence of people in the community of the Liberal faith, including the heads of the organizations, the commissioner was satisfied beyond question and reported that there was not the slightest evidence of this man having been a partisan.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT WITH RESPECT TO DISMISSALS
speechtext: When was the commissioner appointed?

maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT WITH RESPECT TO DISMISSALS
speechtext:
Not until 1934, I think. The minister, as I say, felt that this was an old matter which should not be reopened, but the man was so insistent, putting it on that ground, not asking for compensation but seeking only to vindicate his own reputation that an investigation was ordered. Officers of the Indian department on the spot were examined, and many others, including the mayor of the
Dismissals-Mr. Bennett

town, the former Indian agent, merchants and others, who had been associated with the complainant-the minister of the church who was there at the time, and those who had had to do with this Indian agent in the closest way. One of them, a lawyer and the secretary of the Liberal Association at the time this occurred, went so far as to say that he had no personal knowledge of the man being active politically, that in fact he "considered him quiet in that respect." One of them went so far as to say that if there had been any partisanship on his part he at least would have heard of it; and he had not.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT WITH RESPECT TO DISMISSALS
speechtext:
Would the right hon.
gentleman give the name?

maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT WITH RESPECT TO DISMISSALS
speechtext:
Yes, but I wondered
whether it was desirable to give names. The name of the man was MacConnell, of Kam-sack, Saskatchewan. The former minister endeavoured to escape, as I say, but finally an appointment was made; the report was not made until January, 1935, at Kelvington, Saskatchewan, and they all agreed that there was not the slightest evidence of political partisanship on the part of this unfortunate man who lost his job. I think the difficulty arose because of the fact that after his dismissal he held a position under the provincial government as liquor vendor or something of that sort, and there was confusion as to the two positions. That may explain it in part. At any rate I have given the facts as shown on the record.
Under these circumstances I suggest that in all cases of this kind the rule should be laid down by the government, consequent upon a certificate being given by a member that to his personal knowledge-although Sir Wilfrid Laurier said he should recite the facts-an employee of the crown had been guilty of partisanship, and the employee denying it in toto, the government should grant him the right of investigation. I do not wish to go farther than that at this time, because I realize that this is a matter about which there has been much controversy and which has been discussed at various times. But I go so far as to say that where a man has been removed, on certificate given to the minister by a member of this house, if he makes denial immediately upon being made acquainted with the fact that he has been removed in consequence of such complaint he should be accorded the privilege of investigation. That is all I ask. I might go farther, because I believe there are certain consequences or implications which arise, but I believe my request is reasonable. Certainly we endeavoured to act on that principle.
JMr. Bennett.]

maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT WITH RESPECT TO DISMISSALS
speechtext: Does he not have his recourse before a court of justice?

maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT WITH RESPECT TO DISMISSALS
speechtext:
That is an open question. But how can a poor unfortunate man be driven to court and to consultation with lawyers on these questions when probaibly he is making only a poor subsistence for himself and his family? He has not the money with which to consult lawyers; he has not the money with which to carry on litigation. But if he is accorded an investigation, all would be well. No member of parliament should complain for a single moment against an investigation of his certificate when a man denies validity of the charge made against him. I do not think any hon. member would consider such investigation unfair.
The other point to which I wish to direct attention arises out of the same matter. Numbers of men holding positions have been let out, and others have taken their places. Some of those dismissals have been made under great hardship, because the returned man's preference has been swept aside. I will not go into the cases before me in detail, but I have been asked to bring the facts to the attention of the house as strongly as possible. These facts affect a number of men who occupied positions in the public service. For instance, a returned man, whose name I shall not use unless I am asked, who had worked for a long time in the Prescott elevator, has been replaced by a man who, to use the expression of the complainant "while I was fighting for my country, was stealing from his country," the present employee having stolen from the mails and having been sentenced to the penitentiary. This man now occupies the position formerly held by the returned soldier. I ask any hon. member how he would feel under like circumstances.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT WITH RESPECT TO DISMISSALS
speechtext: I would ask the right hon. gentleman to give me a memorandum respecting the situation he has just mentioned. I was not aware that any man had been replaced in the Prescott elevator, for any cause.

maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT WITH RESPECT TO DISMISSALS
speechtext:
I will gladly give the minister a memorandum. I shall not mention any names unless I am asked to do so, because I feel that in some sense such action might result in handicapping the man's position, and if at all possible I desire to avoid doing that. As a matter of fact I have three complaints. One man puts his case this way: "While I was offering my life for my country, the man who succeeded me was stealing from my country. He was convicted for theft from the mails, and served two years in the penitentiary." Now this unfortunate complainant is walking about without a position, and naturally he

Dismissals-Mr. Bennett
feels keenly his present circumstances. Then, a second man, I am sorry to say, has been succeeded by one who did time. I am not raising the issue because men have done time and should therefore be precluded from reestablishing themselves, but I am saying that returned men are entitled to different treatment, not because I suggest it but because the statute says so. That is the reason. Do not for one moment think that I do not appreciate the difficulties the government faces. For instance, I do not believe that the Minister of Railways and Canals would for one moment sanction such conditions; but these are the facts. How they have developed, or how they have been brought about, is not for me at this time to discuss.
Then, I have another case which touches the Department of Railways and Canals. This is one affecting a man who had been working two or three years in the department. It is only fair to the hon. member for York North (Mr. Mulock) to say that this man might be classified as a temporary employee. However he had a position in the department, and had seen long service. He served in the South African war, in the Zulu war and in the great war. Before the war he was what might be described as a bridge man, and had been given a position of lesser importance on the Welland canal. However, only a few days ago he found himself deprived of that position and succeeded by one who had not any such creditable service. This man is very much incensed and resentful about it. I shall give the facts to the Minister of Railways and Canals because if I were to discuss the matter in the sense in which I should like to discuss it I might prejudice a position which I desire to assist.
Other cases have come to my attention during the session. Letters dealing with some of them have been brought down. One is in the far west, one is in the far east, and so on But in connection with all these cases conditions develop, not because of a desire on the part of the government but because there is not an opportunity for the government to deal with every phase of a matter. That is what I desire to point out.
One of the men about whom I have spoken had worked for three years as leg operator at the Prescott elevator. From 1914 to 1919 he served in the great war, and has been replaced by a man whose name I shall not give, but who was convicted of robbing the mails and as a result served two years in the penitentiary. The man who succeeded the former employee is not a returned soldier. Another case to which I referred affects a man who had held a similar position at Prescott, and who has been replaced by one who was formerly convicted
and served a sentence. The last case to which I referred affects a man who served in the Canadian artillery and who was in the Zulu revolution. In 1912 he went to Natal and joined the Natal Light Horse.

maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT WITH RESPECT TO DISMISSALS
speechtext: How old is he?

maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT WITH RESPECT TO DISMISSALS
speechtext: I do not know.

maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT WITH RESPECT TO DISMISSALS
speechtext: Is he not about seventy years old?

maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT WITH RESPECT TO DISMISSALS
speechtext: No. There are men who have served their country continuously since 1900 who are not seventy years old. He was discharged in Hamilton early in July, 1919, and on April 11 of this year was replaced, through a patronage committee which did not have a returned man on it, by a single man without a war record.

maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT WITH RESPECT TO DISMISSALS
speechtext: Is that the man on the Welland canal?

maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT WITH RESPECT TO DISMISSALS
speechtext:
Yes. The minister to whom he has appealed has been making some investigation. In this instance the minister to whom the appeal has been made is the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Power), not the Minister of Railways and Canal's (Mr. Howe). The minister has been making certain investigations, and there the matter stands.
There are large numbers of these Canadians to whom I might direct attention, but my doing so would serve no useful purpose because I desire only to describe conditions which I believe require the taking of two steps: (1) Where the action taken by a member has resulted in the loss of a position by a civil servant, such servant should have an opportunity for investigation if he denies the correctness of the allegations made, and (2) we should continue to give effect to the provisions in our law with respect to returned men. Particular care should be exercised in placing those who, not having served in the overseas forces violated the criminal laws of the country during the absence of those whose positions they have taken. I think that is not too strong a position to take. I trust that I may present this grievance before we proceed with supply, in order that the government may be advised as to what the conditions are. I feel sure they will take such steps as may be necessary to protect those who desire only what Sir Wilfrid Laurier described as the opportunity to be heard before they are deprived of their positions.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT WITH RESPECT TO DISMISSALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall not attempt to review what my right hon. friend

Dismissals-Mr. Mackenzie King
(Mr. Bennett) has said, for the simple reason that, as all hon. members know, there is probably no more controversial question than that which relates to appointments to and dismissals from the public service. That is my first reason for not attempting at this time to go into the different cases which he has mentioned.

maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT WITH RESPECT TO DISMISSALS
speechtext: I would not expect the right hon. gentleman to do so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT WITH RESPECT TO DISMISSALS
speechtext: In the second place, I do not feel that it is necessary to do so because in all that my right hon. friend has said he has not intimated that the government itself has departed in any way from the principle which he has enunciated as the one that previous administrations-

maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT WITH RESPECT TO DISMISSALS
speechtext: Oh, yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT WITH RESPECT TO DISMISSALS
speechtext: -followed or were supposed to follow, namely that of taking the word of a member of parliament with' respect to dismissals for political partisanship and acting upon it without further question. My right hon. friend is now laying down, for the present administration, a course of action which I do not think was followed by himself-

maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT WITH RESPECT TO DISMISSALS
speechtext: Oh, yes; we gave an investigation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT WITH RESPECT TO DISMISSALS
speechtext: -during the time he was in office. In the five years that my right hon. friend was in office there were, according to a return that was submitted to this house on June 10, no less than 6,352 dismissals from the public service. Of this number, as many as 1,370 were from the Department of the Interior, 1,600 from the Department of Marine, and 1,093 from the Post Office Department. But that does not begin to indicate the extent to which changes were made in the public service which resulted in men being dismissed or losing their positions without having any investigation at all.

maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT WITH RESPECT TO DISMISSALS
speechtext:
Will the right hon. gentleman allow me to ask him how many of those were dismissed because of reorganization?
Mr.. MACKENZIE KING: I am coming to that.

maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT WITH RESPECT TO DISMISSALS
speechtext: We abolished the positions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT WITH RESPECT TO DISMISSALS
speechtext:
My hon. friend asks how many were due to reorganization. Perhaps I cannot better illustrate in what fashion they were due to any "reorganization" than by giving figures with respect to the Department of Agriculture. According to the

figures brought down there were 187 dismissals from that department. There was another return with respect to appointments in the same department, which showed that the number of appointments made in the Department of Agriculture was 2,725.

maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT WITH RESPECT TO DISMISSALS
speechtext: That figure is cumulative, of course. Those were temporary from year to year.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT WITH RESPECT TO DISMISSALS
speechtext: No doubt that was "reorganization."

maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT WITH RESPECT TO DISMISSALS
speechtext: No, no; that was merely from year to year, covering temporary employees who came in during the spring and went out in the fall.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT WITH RESPECT TO DISMISSALS
speechtext:
I do not want to go into this in any controversial spirit, because I believe my right hon. friend himself has been careful to avoid that. Moreover there is no opportunity at the present of hearing the other side of the cases cited or from the hon. members concerned. Further, at an earlier stage in the session I intimated that at the beginning of next session the government would ask the house to appoint a special committee to go into the whole question of appointments and dismissals under the Civil Service Act. That will be the time, I think, when matters of this kind can be taken up and gone into more fully and carefully.
That covers, I think, all I wished more particularly to say, namely that the course which my right hon. friend is now suggesting is not one which, up to the present, has been regarded as in accordance with the general practice. I do not wish to say that there may not be much to be said in support of the position taken by my right hon. friend. Where it can be shown that anyone has been dismissed from the public service obviously without any cause, as long as we have such a thing as justice, which is what above all else government stands for, the government would desire and wish to see that justice was done.

maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT WITH RESPECT TO DISMISSALS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT WITH RESPECT TO DISMISSALS
speechtext: I cannot do more than say to my right hon. friend that the government will be glad, during the period of the recess, to consider carefully the representations he has made. As to indicating what further action, if any, it may be advisable to take, that will have to await a more favourable opportunity for intimating the results to the house.

maintopic: SOCKEYE SALMON INDUSTRY-CLOSING OP HATCHERIES IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
SOCKEYE SALMON INDUSTRY-CLOSING OP HATCHERIES IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair I desire to draw to the attention of the government

Sockeye Salmon Industry-Mr. Barber
a matter which is of very great importance owing particularly to developments of the last few weeks. I refer to the sockeye salmon industry, one of our greatest industries in British Columbia. The reason I raise the matter at this time is that an order in council was passed in March which is not, in my opinion, in the best interests of the industry, and particularly now that the United States have accepted the treaty. I present the matter to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the government in the hope that they may decide not to carry out the provisions of that order in council.
The industry to which I refer is a very valuable one. At the present time it is worth something over three million dollars a year; that is as it stands to-day, with a depleted run. It should amount to twenty-five million dollars if we had given attention to it and to the propagation of fish to keep up those runs. The sockeye spawns altogether in Canadian waters. That is one reason why the adjoining states are vitally interested. Without doubt, the restoration of the Fraser represents the greatest conservation project which we in this country have attempted. I draw the attention of the government particularly to the fact that the order in council which was passed on March 2 of this year is based on a report filed with the minister on February 21, 1936. One clause of the order in council reads as follows:
The minister, on the advice of the Deputy-Minister of Fisheries, recommends that when the present season's operations in the abovenamed hatcheries-
Giving a list of ten hatcheries in British Columbia.
-are completed, they be closed, and disposed of to the best advantage, and that the employees be then retired under the conditions imposed by law.
That action has been taken. I think it must be admitted that it is very drastic, when one considers that the two countries are about to come together under this treaty with the idea of helping this industry and trying to provide that the run of salmon be increased.
The fight for the preservation of the sockeye has been going on for some forty years. I think it was in 1922 that -a commission was appointed to investigate the sockeye salmon industry in the province of British Columbia. This commission filed its report in 1922. The Department of Fisheries prepared a memorandum based on an interim report issued by this commission. In section
15 of that interim report the commission stated:
15. Hatcheries.-Your commission has gone into this matter very thoroughly and heard a great deal of evidence both from employees of the said hatcheries and men engaged in the fishing industry, both as fishermen and purchasers of fish, and we are of the opinion that most of the hatchery operations could be suspended except that two hatcheries be kept in operation to experiment with the new proposed system and that a certain amount of the moneys now spent in hatchery operations be used for the clearing of streams, obstructions in rivers and improving the spawning grounds for natural propagation.
In this memorandum, to which I have referred, the department in reply proceeded to make out a case for the hatcheries. They referred to the fact that during the sittings of the commission only two hatchery employees were called, and they were connected with small hatcheries. I shall not read this memorandum in full, but I should like to quote from page 1 as follows:
There are twelve hatcheries in British Columbia in "which there are several men who have had much longer experience in hatchery operations than Messrs. Catt and Reid, who. however, are both good officers. The district inspector of hatcheries for British Columbia and Major Motherwell, chief inspector of fisheries, could have given authentic and valuable information regarding results that are apparent from British Columbia hatcheries generally.
They then go on to show that from the official records the hatcheries have played a wonderful part in keeping up the runs.

maintopic: SOCKEYE SALMON INDUSTRY-CLOSING OP HATCHERIES IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: What memorandum is the hon. member reading from?

maintopic: SOCKEYE SALMON INDUSTRY-CLOSING OP HATCHERIES IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
This is a memorandum
issued in connection with the interim report of the fisheries commission concerning hatcheries. Referring to the Skeena river watershed, this statement is made:
It must be appreciated that, with 1,091 salmon gill nets, each 1,200 feet in length and with a depth of 50 meshes, if it were not for some extraordinary measure, which in this case is artificial propagation, there would be no likelihood of the run being maintained.
In connection with the Rivers Inlet area, they have this to say on page 5:
Previous to the establishment of the hatchery sockeye salmon did not run in Meadows creek, which is situated just alongside the hatchery. Bach year since hatchery operations were commenced fry had been liberated from the hatchery in Meadows creek. As a result a splendid run of sockeye has been built up in this creek and a considerable portion of the hatchery collection is obtained each year at this point.
4048	.	COMMONS
Sockeye Salmon Industry-Mr. Barber
On page 6, referring to the Vancouver Island area, the memorandum states:
When the hatchery was established, a considerable area had to be covered in order to secure the required supply of eggs. The fry, up to the last two years, have been liberated directly from the hatchery into the lake. The result has been that now large quantities of returning spawning fish come practically to the hatchery door and are obtained by seining on the lake shore. The greater part of the run of fish to this whole area in many recent years have spawned at this place.
From the foregoing it will be seen that the take of eggs now is from a run built up entirely by the hatchery operations and after the full toll has been taken from it by the commercial fishermen.
The New Westminster hatchery is referred to on page 9 as follows:
In 1916 sockeye fry were taken from the New Westminster hatchery and liberated in tributaries of Kawkawa lake. The stocking continued each year for four years. A good run of fish is now returning to that particular lake each year. Previous to this stocking, no sockeye were known to frequent these streams.
How ill advised are suggestions that hatcheries are responsible for the depletion of the Fraser will be realized from the foregoing. On the other hand it may be pertinently asked wliat the runs would have been in view of the notoriously excessive fishing that has been going on, due to international conditions, if the hatcheries had not been operating.
The following general observations are made:
It has been suggested that hatcheries are only useful for replenishing streams that have been depleted. If this argument is accepted and it is granted that the hatcheries will replenish a depleted stream, it must also be - granted that they will maintain an established run equally as well.
There are numerous streams in British Columbia in which a good run of sockeye at one time occurred and which through overfishing is almost extinct. Artificial means are the only way by which these streams can be replenished and a commercial run reestablished. The existing hatcheries can only look after a portion of these streams and if they are again to be productive the fish cultural service must not only be maintained but must be largely extended.
And again:
Against the present condition of barrenness of these once productive areas where there has . been only natural reproduction, the splendid condition of the lower Fraser, where natural reproduction has been assisted by artificial means, is strong evidence of the efficacy of hatcheries. The run to Pitt lake, where there is a small hatchery, is more than holding its own and the run to the Pemberton district has steadily improved since the hatchery was established there.
And then further along:
With the experience in British Columbia and Alaska there can be no doubt that the sockeye runs will not maintain themselves

against commercial fishing unless fishing operations are so restricted as to imperil the success of the industry and that some assistance must be given nature and this can only be by means of artificial propagation.
It would be interesting to know just what knowledge is possessed by those whose evidence before the British Columbia fisheries commission has not been favourable to fish culture and the extent to which they have personally examined into and studied the conditions that prevail on the spawning grounds and in a sockeye stream, as against those that obtain in a hatchery during the period of incubation.
It is admitted by the sportsmen of the province and the numerous angling associations that hatchery operations with game fish have been eminently successful, and in this connection the introduction of Atlantic salmon at Cow'ielian lake, eastern speckled trout in the Kootenay district and black bass in Christina lake and Vancouver Island points are excellent examples. If such operations are successful with these varieties of fish why should they not be equally successful with sockeye?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SOCKEYE SALMON INDUSTRY-CLOSING OP HATCHERIES IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: What is the date of the report?

maintopic: SOCKEYE SALMON INDUSTRY-CLOSING OP HATCHERIES IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
It is a memorandum based on the interim report of the commission which sat in 1922. The concluding words of the memorandum are as follows:
One argument which is very eloquent is the fact that for hundreds of years hatchery operations have been carried on in some of the oldest countries of the world, and they are sufficiently satisfied with results to continue such operations.
Although the federal government of the United States does not administer and does not derive any revenue from the fisheries, except in Alaska, it operates a large and comprehensive fish cultural service entirely at its own expense, and which extends to nearly every state in the union.
In conclusion it is pointed out that the arguments against hatcheries are all presumptive. On such basis it may fairly be asked why-in view of the fact that the foregoing are points of definite knowledge-hatcheries are not the most effective and economical means known for maintaining our anadromous and inland fisheries.
That is the memorandum prepared by the Department of Fisheries. We have the example of Harrison lake, where 2,500,000 sockeye were planted in 1920. In 1927, when they were due to return, 12,000,000 eggs were taken from a point where there had never been any sockeye . salmon. Surely this is evidence that the hatcheries have helped the Canadian runs. I have here a copy of the report of the Minister of Fisheries in which the superintendent of Cultus lake hatchery on page 12 states that in recent years not only have the runs increased, but the size of the salmon has also increased.
We have had on the coast for a number of years a fish that is not only recognized as

Sockeye Salmon Industry-Mr. Barber
a sport fish but is used extensively in the fresh fish trade and to a certain extent in canning. In this connection I wish to give the house an illustration of what can be done through hatchery methods. I can remember the time some years ago when there were very few steelhead in the rivers leading to Cultus lake. Eggs were secured from other sections and hatched and the fry placed in the creeks. Here are the results, obtained entirely from hatchery methods. In 1932 there were collected from returning steelhead 18.600 eggs; in 1933 , 98,900; in 1934, 125,163; in 1935, 133,560; and when I was home this year they had finished collecting and I was informed that the total collections for 1936 stood at 410,000 eggs. I do not think that one can get better evidence than this of the efficacy of hatcheries, and this is recent evidence. These fish stood the so-called hazards of the sea and returned, and if- this is true of steelhead. it is surely true of sockeye. This, I submit, should surely be satisfactory evidence, and it comes from the department itself, which has carried on this work for a number of years.
I wish now to refer to the order in council, and in this regard I should like to know the reason for this right about face in the department's policy. Perhaps I had better read the order in council:
The committee of the privy council have had before them a report, dated 21st February, 1936, from the Minister of Fisheries, submitting as follows:

The basis of determination as to the efficiency of reproduction in any year was the number of young fish that of their own volition left the lake for the sea. This young sockeye do in the second year of their age and they remain at sea until they reach maturity.
