speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the committee rose at six o'clock, the item under discussion was No. 167, Royal Canadian Mounted Police, pay of force and" so on.

Under this item I should like
to take a few minutes to discuss a matter which has arisen in my district. It is not often that I object to having money spent in the district which I represent, but this is a waste of money. The tale can best be told by consideration of the questions and answers that were submitted to the house to-day, so I shall refer to them briefly first:
Has a station of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police been recently started at Alert Bay?
The answer was yes.
Was there a station of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police at that place about the year 1021?
The answer is:
Yes. It was opened in the first place on the 26th January, 1920.
I may say that it was closed in 1924 on my recommendation. Then I asked:
Since then has there been any considerable increase in the number of crimes committed?
The answer is: No information. Then I asked:
Since then has there been any serious crime committed at that place?
The answer is: No information. Then I asked:
Is there a station of provincial police at Alert Bay?
The answer is yes. Then I asked:
Is there any reason to suppose that they are not competent to handle the enforcement of law in that neighbourhood?
Surely that is a pertinent question, and this is the answer:
They are believed to be competent to handle the situation, but the Department of Indian Affairs reports that the members of the provincial police are too busy with other matters to attend to Indians who are considered federal charges.
If that is true the first part of the answer is incorrect, because in that case they are not competent and are not attending to their duties, but as a matter of fact that is not true. They are thoroughly competent and

have always shown their ability in that
regard. Then I ask:
Before recommending the establishment of a station of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police at that place was the attorney general of British Columbia or the commissioner of police for that province consulted or asked if they were unable to handle the enforcement of the law in that place?
Surely that is a very proper question, in view of the relations that obtain between the dominion and the provinces. If a bargain was made with the province to carry out the enforcement of the law and it was found that the law was not being enforced, surely the proper procedure would be to go to the attorney general and say, "Are you not able to do it? If you are not, we shall have to put in our own men." The answer is:
No, but the conditions complained of were investigated by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and charges were laid and convictions obtained. This seems to bear out the contention that the British Columbia provincial police are too busy to attend to such matters. Furthermore, some of the Indians in the area have become hostile to authority and are alleged to be getting out of hand.
The charges that were laid and the convictions that were obtained were these: The Royal Canadian Mounted Police sent a man up in disguise, and as a result I think three charges were laid against two men, and two or three convictions were obtained. That was the extent of the crime; two men were convicted, and that was the end of the matter. I took it upon myself to write the commissioner of police for British Columbia and ask if he and his force were not capable of handling the situation there. He wrote back to the effect that they were fully competent." His letter continues:
I do not know on whose instructions they were sent, but there are two mounted policemen at Alert Bay at present. We have two constables there ourselves . . . and the game warden is also sworn in as a provincial constable

So we have five constables in that small place. I also asked the provincial police commissioner with regard to this serious increase in crime, these major crimes that have been occurring, and he gives me the record:
During the past two years . . . there were sixty-two cases recorded against white persons and seventy-six against Indians. The great majority of these were minor offences and we have had no serious crime at Alert Bay for a long time.
There were altogether 138 cases, against Indians and whites, which gives an average of one and a quarter a week, with five constables on the job. The commissioner of police says he is fully capable of handling the situation

Supply-Justice-Mounted Police
and would have done so if he had been advised of it. In 1928, I think it was, this same trouble arose again. I had the station closed in 1924, but practically the same element wanted this station reopened. At that time all I did was to recommend that the Minister of Justice apply to the provincial police and ask their opinion. The attorney general promptly wrote back and said, "If we need more men there we will send them, but we are thoroughly competent to handle the situation." Now we are going to start a station there with two men. Again I asked:
Has it been recommended that a barracks should be built for their accommodation?
The answer is no. Probably I used the wrong word when I said "recommended"; I should have said "suggested," and then I think the minister would have had to say yes. At that, a recommendation will come along soon, because once you start a station with two men you must have some place to put them, and there will be a demand. Then I asked:
Were any steps taken to check up on the accuracy of such statements?
The answer was no. No such steps were taken, but this reply shows that the representatives of the Department of Indian Affairs in British Columbia requested the officer commanding the mounted police in that province to establish a detachment at Alert Bay in order to protect the Indians in that area from the sale of intoxicants. At that point the cases average one and a quarter per week for whites and Indians, over a period of two years. When the Royal Canadian Mounted Police took charge and sent in a secret agent, in disguise, they secured three convictions and that was the end of the matter. Since those convictions were obtained there has been no great crime; yet we are going to have five constables in a place of that size.
This all originated with an official out there who thought it would be quite grand to have the mounted police running around with him, in gold lace and uniform, as a sort of glorified bodyguard. That is the whole thing in a nutshell; it cannot be and never has been denied. I have the whole file before me, though I shall not detain the committee by reading it. That is the situation; that is what has been suggested, and I suppose the government will go on with it, but I must make my protest. We are wasting this money; it is not necessary, and it will create ill-will. In 1924, on my advice, that station was closed. I asked if there had been any serious crime since that
time, and the answer was no. I asked if there had been any great increase in crime, and the answer was no. The provincial police are a smart, non-political, uniformed force. Their men are moved around from time to time in order to keep them from getting too familiar with the local people. They are a very capable body, of whom we should be proud, and it is an insult and a slur upon that body of men to say that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police must go in there because the provincial police are too busy- which is another way of saying too inattentive-to look after these people. It is ridiculous to say that the provincial police are too busy, when the cases average only one and a quarter per week. This insult is totally uncalled for, and we are going to be saddled with these expenses simply to gratify the desire of an official to have a glorified bodyguard go around with him.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I may assure my hon. friend that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police are carrying on work in the various provinces throughout the dominion simply at the request of some department of the government, and that is what has been done in this case. The Department of Indian Affairs requested that this detachment be sent to this point. We would be only too glad not to have to send anyone, but we-and when I say "we" I mean the police-receive instructions from the various departments of the government which we have to carry out. Unfortunately, or fortunately, it is from them that we have to take our orders.

That may be so, but I do not think the minister would go so far as to say that he is the servant of any cheap jack department that comes along with a request of any kind. This arose in this way, according to the records, which I shall not take time to read: One of these Indian officials went down to Vancouver-his own letter says so-and saw the head of the British Columbia police. Apparently he said to him, "Captain So and So, wouldn t you like to start a detachment of the mounted police at Alert Bay"? Like all officials, always ready to get a bigger circle of attendants, he said, "Yes, we have a man who is just the very man for the job; we shall be happy to send him in if you say so." And the whole thing was settled. He reported to the Indian department here, and the department without any investigation said, "Yes, it is a good idea," and they planted him on the department. All I can do is to repeat that this was not necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I shall be
pleased to look into the matter. My information does not entirely coincide with what the hon. member has said.

I know something of this as well, and thinking of the two very fine men who fell victims to the assaults of some Indians in British Columbia I made up my mind that we should have to maintain some assistance in Indian reserves to prevent the possibility of repetition of such an event as that which happened in the interior of British Columbia where two mounted police were murdered under terrible circumstances. Wherever there is the possibility of liquor among the Indian population there is need for those who will guard them as our wards.

But may I ask the leader of the opposition: Is it not a fact that the dominion made a bargain with the province to enforce the statutes, which bargain the provincial authorities are willing to carry out? Until they show evidence of failing-
No: there is no such agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The Indian Act is a dominion statute and the province has nothing to do with the enforcement of that.
Carried.
No; the item is not going to carry on an assertion of that sort. Is not the criminal code a dominion statute?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
Do not the provincial police enforce that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes,
because the administration of criminal justice is under the jurisdiction of the provinces; but the enforcement of dominion statutes, our own acts, is under our own control.
Then, why is it that you do not have a station of the mounted police at every Indian village all over the country?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Because it is not necessary and is not requested.

Who does enforce the provisions of the Indian Act in nine out of ten places in British Columbia? It is the provincial police, by request of the dominion government. If I am wrong, the department ought to have a policeman stationed at every village, because wherever there is an Indian there is danger of his getting liquor. It is not correct to say that the enforcement of the Indian Act in British Columbia is confined

to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. I was an Indian agent for ten years, and whenever I wanted a policeman I applied to the provincial authorities who supplied one or more as needed. All this talk about the Indians getting out of hand in that district is nonsense.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I assure my hon. friend that there is a detachment of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in every large Indian community in British Columbia.

Mr. Chairman, while you passed item No. 492 without my having an opportunity -to notice it, I had intended to make an observation or two in respect to it. We listened this afternoon to a very long and bitter attack in connection with these Regina riots, so-called. I think the minister should make a statement on that item.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I might make a statement without reverting to the item. All I want to say in answer to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) who referred to the matter this afternoon,, is that it is always easy to be wise after the event. There is no doubt that long after an event has taken place one can see where something might have been done differently in the light of what has happened. This affair occurred more than a year ago. Fortunately the same troubles do not exist at the present time, and I do not' think it would serve any good purpose to try to find that those who were at that time' faced with a very grave and serious responsiJ bility might perhaps have taken another course than the one they did take. All I wish to say with regard to the many statements made this afternoon is that I was especially interested in what the judges, who were appointed not by this government but by the Saskatchewan government to inquire into that serious matter-which was very regrettable because one man was killed and many were injured-found in regard to what the police did in those circumstances. On page 288 of the judges' report I find this:
In our report we have dealt with as many of the cases as we believed merited it and have reached the conclusion that although the police used force on a number of occasions it was so used either to repel attack or to overcome resistance to arrest, and that in no case was there reliable evidence of an unprovoked assault by a member of either force.
Then I want to call attention more particularly to this part of the report, at page 303:
An effort was made by some of the witnesses to create the impression that the Royal Cana-

Supply-Justice*-Mounted Police
dian Mounted Police have deteriorated from their earlier standards. As to the character of the men at present in the force Colonel Wood stated that under present conditions it had been possible to procure a type of men "superior to anything we have had in the force for the past thirty or forty years." And he added, "I have lived in barracks all my life." Several thousand applications are received each year and only a small quota is selected twice a year. A written examination is required and an investigation into the character of each applicant is conducted. Many members of the force, both officers and men, appeared before us and the impression made upon us does not bear out the criticism levelled at the present force.
We are of the opinion that Colonel Wood during all the time the strikers were in Saskatchewan acted with care and moderation, always of course bearing in mind the orders from his superior officer which he was bound to obey. We think also that the members of the force as a whole acted with courage and marked restraint during the riot and this notwithstanding the fact that they were repeatedly engaged in repelling attacks which were characterized by viciousness, brutality and a disregard for human life.
And at page 311:
We think it may be said, to put it mildly, that the men from the camps were most unfortunate in placing their cause in the hands of such leadership. The evidence indicates that a percentage of the men were lawless and dangerous. On the other hand we have reason to believe that the majority of them were of a different type and call for sympathetic consideration. The leaders, however, gave the whole movement a colour and character which condemned it from its inception and which caused it to be branded as dangerous by those in authority, who are responsible for the preservation of the peace, order and good government of the country.
All I have to say is that we must consider with justice and fairness, but with a little sympathy, the positions of those who are placed in offices of responsibility in times of trouble and difficulty like the occasion of the spring of 1935, and we must do our best to strengthen the hands of those who have, after all, to maintain peace and order in Canada. On the whole I do not think the evidence as given in the investigation carried out at Regina, and the report which was presented by impartial commissioners, members of the high court of justice in Saskatchewan-

There was one county
court judge.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes;
there was one county court judge. I do not think the country has to be humiliated in any wav by the part played by those who had to take responsibility at that time.

I deprecate very greatly the province undertaking to inquire into the conduct of federal affairs. This is a new
precedent in the constitutional history of Canada. But it was done, and I can only point out that there was not continuity of government, when the commission was sitting, as between the dates of the events.
I was not asked to be heard. The former Minister of Justice was not asked to be heard. We were not represented either in person or by counsel1. I was told I was to be asked to attend. I was not asked. The attempt made to indicate that members of a government undertook to direct proceedings with respect to what happened at Regina, a long distance away from Ottawa, is entirely unwarranted.
But the principle of a province appointing a commission to investigate the conduct of the federal government is a dangerous precedent and will in the end, in my judgment, create great difficulty in the operation of our constitutional system. I have only to point out that a few days ago a man was killed in British Columbia, and the prisoner was sent up for trial. He was charged with murder, in the first instance, but the charge was reduced to manslaughter, and when the case came up for trial the attorney general discontinued it. I shall just read this statement from a Vancouver newspaper and ask the Minister of Justice whether he thinks we should not appoint a commission to investigate this matter. The article reads:
New Westminster, May 14.-A stay of proceedings in the charge of manslaughter against Louise Rosse resulting from the death of R. A. Hanna after a drinking party and brawl in a Port Coquitlam hotel last month was requested by H. J. Sullivan, crown counsel, in assize court to-day. Chief Justice Morrison granted the stay and freed Rosse, who has been awaiting trial on $15,000 bail. Rosse and Gordon Wismer, his counsel, appeared in court. Mr. Sullivan then announced that the Attorney General had authorized him to apply for stay of proceedings.
At the preliminary hearing evidence was given that Hanna, well known Maple Ridge resident and oil agent, had died of hemorrhage of the brain after being struck in a fight by Rosse, hotelkeeper, following a card game quarrel.
And that man has never been tried before a jury of the people. There has been no investigation, except before a magistrate, and yet there is no means, except by the appointment of a royal commission, to investigate as to how the man's life was taken.
What date?

The article is dated
May 14.

Is that
all the information my right hon. friend has about the case, namely, what he has obtained from the New Westminster paper?

It was taken from the paper. I am reading it from a newspaper clipping.
Has my right hon. friend no further information?

Except that a man was killed. And I was told, also, that he was killed. But it does not matter in what circumstance he was killed; there should have been a judicial investigation. This afternoon the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre made some complaints to the effect that certain men had been convicted. They were convicted by a jury. They were found guilty by a jury. All sympathy and all appeals that could be brought to bear were attended to by counsel, and yet they were tried and found guilty by a jury.
Now, the question of divided jurisdiction is nowhere so important as it is with respect to criminal law. In this house on more than one occasion competent men, men who have not been members of the legal profession, have urged strongly that there should be some provision for the federal power exercising jurisdiction in the discussion of cases before the courts of the country. That at the present time is not the law. But as a result of a province appointing a royal commission to investigate into the workings of the federal power it should follow that the federal power could appoint a commission to investigate the workings in the provinces, which, of course, would be injurious to the working of the whole machinery of government.
Bnt on the other hand if a complaint is made that a man's life is lost, and you enter a nolle prosequi, and the accused is not proceeded against, it matters not what the facts are, I say, that there should be a judicial and public investigation as to the circumstances which brought about that result.
Was there a coroner's inquest?
I do not know; there was a preliminary investigation. The man was sent up for trial, and the charge was reduced to manslaughter. He was given bail, and-
My right hon. friend is surely not condemning the proceedings by virtue of what he has read in the press.

I know this, that this man was not tried, and a man was killed by him. That is the important point; he killed a man, and he was not tried. It is the only time I have ever seen that done in this country.

I object to this proceeding. The right hon. gentle-

man has only a newspaper version of what happened.
No; complaint was made to me about the affair, and the statement was made that this matter should be discussed.
That is different. May I ask my right hon. friend if he received complaints with regard to this particular case?
Yes.
Could he read the letter?
That is the reason this clipping wras sent to me; that is the reason I have it.
Mr. Chairman, honestly I must protest against this.
Why protest?
Because by inference my right hon. friend is condemning the administration of justice in British Columbia, and is condemning it on a mere press report.
Yes; but I say this, that a preliminary investigation was held before a justice of the peace; the case was sent to trial and nothing further has been done about it.
That is never final.

But there was never a chance to investigate the circumstances under which this life was lost; that is my complaint. It is a precedent that is established, and I here put myself on record, protesting to the Attorney General of Canada that they should have opened up the case, because I believe the circumstances were such that it was not a proper exercise of powers of a province to set up an investigation over the federal government, any more than the federal government should investigate the operations of a provincial government.
Now, what happened? As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said this afternoon, the leaders were not proceeded against. Evans was not proceeded against. The other leaders to whom reference was made in the report were not proceeded against. But the smaller fry were convicted by verdict of a jury and, as the hon. member said, were sentenced. I say that that is not proper; it is not the proper course to pursue, in view of what has happened. That is all I have said.

speechtext:
And
there had been loss of life. Under our law everything concerning murder and any other criminal matters is under the jurisdiction of the provinces. Surely it was the right of the province of Saskatchewan, indeed it was its business, to investigate into all that surrounded this painful occurrence, and this was done judicially and in a way that, I believe, has contributed to let the public of Canada know better what were the circumstances. At the opening of the session I told my right hon. friend that I thought it was in the interest of everybody, the police, the government and all of those who had anything to do with the matter, that it should be fully investigated. I had the greatest confidence in the personnel of the commission. I am glad that this report has been given out to the public of Canada, and I cannot understand why this should be criticized and why my right hon. friend should think it would have been better to allow the various rumours and reports that were circulated to remain uninvestigated and unanswered. It would not have been for the good of the authorities or in the interests of peace and order that the public should have been kept in ignorance of the real facts.

I think the hon. gentleman has not quite appreciated my point. There was provision made for a judicial investigation, ' because several men were charged with the commission of offences, and it is the duty of the courts to make inquiry at a properly constituted court. That is the point; and while such a court was available- and in the end that proceeding had to take place-a commission was set up, consisting in part of judges who might and would in the ordinary course have to deal with this judicially, and investigated it from another angle altogether. If a charge is made against a person, and the courts are there for the purpose of holding the fullest investigation,

and that investigation must ultimately take place in the courts of the country, why have a commission of judges appointed to investigate the circumstances in connection with the event, the striking of the men, the circumstances under which the rioting took place, before the judicial trial takes place and an opportunity is afforded to investigate the matter in the manner and form by law provided? Surely we have created a most dangerous precedent. That is the point I endeavoured to make, based upon a strong opinion I hold which has nothing to do with this case at all. I suppose there is hardly anyone in this house who does not remember what took place in India when General Dyer found himself in difficulties. He came to England and brought action against those who libelled him, and he succeeded, with the aid of a jury, in recovering his reputation and damages. The late Mr. Justice McCardie dealt with the matter at great length in a judgment which is a classic of its kind. But to prejudice the judicial hearing by a prior investigation, and then to have the authorities that have set up the commission nolle prosequi the proceedings against the leaders and proceed against others, and the jury convict, them, and the judges, having regard to the circumstances set out this afternoon, give them a light sentence-I say that creates a dangerous precedent and one upon which I should like a discussion on another occasion, though not, for the reasons I have stated, at the present time.

As the one responsible for appointing the commission I desire to say a word or two. The commission was not appointed in the first instance for the purpose of examining into what was referred to by the leader of the opposition. In 1927, while I was premier of Saskatchewan, I came to Ottawa and arranged with the federal government to have the mounted police force police that province. We were the first province in Canada to make an arrangement of this kind: since that time the majority of the provinces have followed suit. In 1935 the riot took place at Regina, and there was some controversy between the dominion government and the provincial government as to jurisdiction. We claimed that we had the right to direct the mounted police in dealing with this particular trouble. The federal government took it upon themselves to direct the police.
The hon. gentleman might give the reason, too.

After the men had arrived at Regina and the issue was drawn we remained out of the contest until final

action, the riot, took place. When the riot was over and the men were gone from Regina, having been moved out by the government of the province, the province then appointed a commission to investigate, and one of the directions given was to investigate the relationships existing between the provincial government and the federal government towards the mounted police force. The agreement which was made in 1927 came into effect in 1928, and1 comes to an end in 1938. It was thought wise that the legal position of the province and the federal government should be known before a new agreement was drawn up. After the commission had been appointed, other matters were referred to it, upon requests from the men and others. This was done to clear up the whole matter. It has been cleared up, in my opinion fairly satisfactorily to all parties concerned. I have nothing further to say at the moment with regard to it, but if the subject is to be discussed at a later time we can probably go into all questions connected with it.

There was a provision in the agreement preserving to the dominion government the right to deal with breaches of dominion statutes, as the Minister of Justice has mentioned. It was in furtherance' of that agreement and the statute that the mounted police, when complaints were made and a request was made upon them by the railways, took the action they did to protect the property of the federal railways. The reasons were given in this house.

I shall detain the committee only a minute. The minister's conception of provincial responsibilities for enforcing the law appears to have broadened to some extent since the last item we were discussing. I must contradict that.

The question of the marketing of coarse grains is becoming almost as important as that concerning the marketing of wheat. I shall not take the time to go into the comparative values of coarse grains from the feeding standpoint, as sufficient figures have been placed on Hansard during this session by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader), and during last session by the then member for Souris, Mr. Willis. That would take too long, but I should like to read briefly from a memorandum which was sent to me. Following the discussion we had on the resolution which stood in my name on the order paper early in the session, I received the following memorandum:
One of the counterbalancing factors influencing farmers in planning their acreage to be sowm to barley is the cash return per acre. The superiority which barley possesses over other cereals in producing additional live stock food value per acre will make an appeal to the cereal producer who is growing cereals for feed purposes on his own farm, but will have little attraction to the farmer producing the cereal as a cash crop.
The two principal reasons why barley is not more extensively grown as a straight cash crop are: first, unfair grading, which results in too small a proportion of the crop earning whatever premium may be carried by malting or export bai-ley, i.e., that is the trade does, not in any year pay the premium for all the barley they export or turn to the malting companies; and second, the price to the farmer of ninety per cent of the barley grown in Canada in any year is governed entirely by the export price of from two to six, and not in any season exceeding ten per cent, of the crop produced.
The farmers in western Canada, particularly those in the southern halves of the three prairie provinces, were forced last year to market their coarse grains because of the destruction of the wheat crop by rust. The price at which they were forced to sell their coarse grains in order to get some money with which to carry on was very low; in fact it was unprecedently low. I have in my possession a letter which I received the other day from a farmer in the Wolseley district. This man farms two or three sections of land and last year he lost most of his wheat crop through rust. He told me that in order to get a forty gallon barrel of gasoline he had .to sell seventy bushels of barley.
Following the short discussion which took place on the resolution that stood in my name on the order paper I received many
letters endorsing the proposal that coarse grains should be brought under the Canadian Wheat Board Act. I also received copies of resolutions which had been passed by boards of trade, pool organizations and municipal organizations. Section 14 of the wheat board act provides for bringing coarse grains undfer the operation of the act by order in council after a recommendation by the wheat board to the government. The machinery is already set up, and I think it is important that this action should be taken. I trust the government will give this matter its consideration immediately. It is important that the step should be taken in time so that the farmers will have an opportunity of marketing their coarse grains under the act when the new crop comes on the market. I do not want to delay the committee and I regret that we have to discuss this very important matter so late in the session. I know many hon. members of this committee, particularly those from western Canada, will endorse this proposal. I hope that as soon as parliament prorogues they will bring what pressure they can to bear upon the government to have them take this problem into consideration.
There is just one other matter I should like to discuss. I may be a little out of order, but much time has been taken up to-day in discussing matters that were really out of order. I should like to direct attention to the fact that in western Canada a great many organizations are anxious that the board should handle the 1936 crop and that a minimum price should be set at an early date. The crop year ends on July 31, and I think it is important that this price should be set in good time. Last year a delay occurred because of certain necessities, but this year the machinery is set up, the board is in operation and there is no reason why a price should not be set in good time.
I should like to bring to the attention of the committee and the government three resolutions which have been passed recently in Saskatchewan. They suggest that the board continue and that a price of 87i cents or better per bushel be fixed at as early a date as possible. When the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) this morning asked a question on the orders of the day, the minister informed him that he would have a statement to make with respect to what the government had in mind in view of what has happened to the Natural Products Marketing Act. Is the minister prepared to make that statement now?

I am not in a position to announce the policy of the government on this matter in view of the fact that since the supreme court brought down the decision there has been no time to give consideration to it in council. I can only say that there is a possibility that the matter may be carried to the privy council, in which event the act will remain, as I understand it, pretty much in the same position as it has been since the question was referred to the supreme court. If that is not the case, the government intends to carry on in connection with marketing in a manner which will assist the marketing of these different products. As regards fruit, it is the view of the department that in the Fruit Act itself the minister has power to do most of the things which an export board had power to do under the marketing act, which has been declared ultra vires; at least, though part of it has not really been declared ultra vires, the fact that other sections have been thrown out renders the act as a whole invalid. But we have power, so far as fruits are concerned, to act pretty much in the same way as the export board could have acted under that legislation. It is not thought there will be great difficulty in doing the things we want to do with regard to fruit. In connection with other matters the intention is to use the sum now before the committee for the purpose of promoting marketing in the interval.

It is quite probable, as the minister says, that with regard to the export of fruit it will be possible under the Fruit Act to do at least a certain amount of valuable work. Certainly it will not be possible, under the Fruit Act, to carry out control work such as the boards have been doing. I should like to say that to me the judgment is not intelligible, particularly that portion which occurs in the middle. I read the middle paragraph:
Regulation of individual trades, or trades in individual commodities in this sweeping fashion-
Referring to the earlier language of the judgment.
-is not competent to the parliament of Canada and such a scheme of regulation is not prac-

ticable in view of the distribution of legislative powers enacted by the constitution act, without the cooperation of the provincial legislatures

In this matter that is exactly what we have. In British Columbia there was a statute passed for the purpose of dovetailing into this very act, and where the judgment says there is a lack of cooperation on the part of the provinces, certainly that cannot apply to British Columbia. There, as the minister knows, the British Columbia tree fruit growers had the most prominent and possibly the most successful of these boards. At the present time, not unnaturally, the members of that board do not know what their position is.
I wonder whether the minister would amplify his statement a little with regard to the possibility and desirability of assisting a case to be carried through the courts, if necessary to the privy council. My idea is that the only thing to be done at the present time is for the board to prosecute the first infringement which comes to its notice and, if necessary, carry the case through the courts up to the privy council. It is obvious that the tree fruit board, subsisting as it is now on what remains of the levies on last year's crop, cannot finance such a procedure. So I should like to know to what extent the dominion government would be prepared to assist, if that be the course considered desirable by all concerned, in order to carry the matter through. I have a strong feeling that if this act had not been thrown to the supreme court holus-bolus, the act being in operation at this time and boards being in operation under it all over Canada, but rather if a concrete case had been taken to the supreme court and argued by capable counsel, it is not at all unlikely that the judgment would not have been similar to this sweeping judgment. This judgment is based upon the statement that there is no legislative assistance on the part of the provinces, and certainly with regard to British Columbia that is contrary to the facts.

Just before the minister speaks, I believe the judgment of the supreme court was inadequately reported in the statement that appeared on the day the judgments were delivered. I have been told that that is so; that these words appeared in the precis that was given out:
Regulation of individual trades, or trades in individual commodities in this sweeping fashion, is not competent to the parliament of Canada and such a scheme of regulation is not practicable in view of the distribution of legislative powers enacted by the constitution act, without the cooperation of the provincial legislatures-

The words from "in" to "legislatures" are quoted in this precis. The preceding paragraph, to which reference is made, reads:
The powers of regulation vested in the commissions extend to external trade and matters connected therewith and to trade in matters of interprovineial concern; but also to trade which is entirely local and of purely local concern.
That, the precis says, may not be carried on except with the cooperation of the provincial legislatures. Nothing was clearer than that this statute never would1 have come into being but for that fact. It was never intended in this house to provide a code for marketing that extended to purely local transactions. The act says distinctly that it refers only to interprovineial and external trade, and local trade is regulated by provincial legislatures. If the local legislature empowered this local board to ask the federal board to act as its agent, or if the federal board asked the local board to act as its agent, that might be done. That is the position, and when this act was passed it was for the sole purpose of coordinating the efforts of the federal and provincial powers in order to secure a marketing act. It would be news indeed to every member of this house to learn that this parliament cannot deal with the licensing of imports and exports; that it cannot deal with interprovineial trade, solely and exclusively, and that it cannot deal with foreign trade outside Canada in any way it pleases. If such were the case, we would have entirely to revise our conception of the constitution.
I am sorry the Minister of Justice is not present, but when I urged that he should not have referred the marketing act to the courts because it was really in operation, that to do so was contrary to every well established and recent precedent, I had in mind the words used by the privy council in the case of the attorney general for Ontario v. the Hamilton Street Railway Company:
With regard to the remaining questions, which it has been suggested should be reserved for further argument, their lordships are of opinion that it would be inexpedient and contrary to the established practice of this board to attempt to give any judicial opinion upon those questions. They are questions proper to be considered in concrete cases only; and opinions expressed upon the operation of the sections referred to, and the extent to which they are applicable, would be worthless for many reasons.
We at least had high authority for saying such opinions would be worthless.
They would be worthless as being speculative opinions on hypothetical questions. It would be contrary to principle, inconvenient, and inexpedient that opinions should be given upon such questions at all. When they arise, they must arise in concrete cases, involving private

Supply-Agriculture-M arketing
rights; and it would be extremely unwise for any judicial tribunal to attempt before hand to exhaust all possible cases and facts which might occur to qualify, cut down, and override the operation of particular words when the concrete case is not before it.
Those are the words of the privy council, but notwithstanding that this government referred this matter to the supreme court, though the act was in operation. Those words dealing with concrete cases never had greater application than they have to this act to-day, namely that it would be extremely unwise for any judicial tribunal to attempt beforehand to exhaust all possible cases and facts which might occur to qualify, cut down, and override the operation of particular words when the concrete case is not before it.
Under those circumstances, having regard to that precedent, I suggest that this is a worthless opinion. Those are not my words at all; that is what the privy council have said;
They are questions proper to be considered in concrete cases only; and opinions expressed upon the operation of the sections referred to, and the extent to which they are applicable, would be worthless for many reasons. They would be worthless as being speculative opinions on hypothetical questions.
I say to the minister and to this committee that if to-day we had a concrete case from the Okanagan and we were able to show the concrete facts as we would be in any case that might be brought before the courts, as in the British Columbia case of the Crystal Dairy, we would be able to prove that there was a local board; that there was a federal board; that there was a provincial statute and a dominion statute; that there was cooperation between the two, and that the two together made a perfect code to deal with the marketing of fruit in that particular locality. Under those circumstances, taking the words of the court as they appear in this opinion, from the standpoint of the concrete facts that must arise in connection with the administration of the marketing act, I suggest to the minister that the proper course to pursue is to take an appeal in order that this language of the privy council may have full application; or not to take an appeal at this moment on the general question but to take an appeal on a concrete case and, as my hon. friend and former colleague from Yale has suggested, let the dominion government undertake to pay the cost, which is not an unusual thing to do. In other words, let a proceeding be taken in the Okanagan valley at once, on an infringement. Let all the facts be proven as to the constitution of the local boards, for the minister doubtless will recall-because
he has had to do with the question in his own province'

that when the Crystal Dairy case came up it was held by the privy council that inasmuch as it provided for a levy being made it was beyond the competence of that legislature to enact that form of taxation. That was the decision of the privy council.
Now we have a case in which infringement of this act may be set up, the facts proven, the local board, the dominion act, the dominion board, the coordination between the two. Then, by special leave, the case can be taken at once, per saltern as we say, to the privy council; we can get it there for early decision so that the question may be settled as to the validity of the sections which deal with concrete facts and not speculative opinions. I cannot say how much I regret that an act which has been in operation should have been referred to the court in the face of the declaration of the privy council which I have just read. But this has been done and we have this judgment in the terms in which we have it. I have not any doubt that this parliament must have power to deal with matters of trade that affect interprovincial transactions or transactions with foreign countries. But the extent to which we may do so through the doctrine of agency and by cooperation between provincial legislatures and boards set up by provincial authority and boards functioning under authority of the federal act is a matter which might well require further argument in order that there might be an ultimate decision by the court of last resort. I urge that on the minister, because having regard to the circumstances I think it is what he would do if he were a private individual. Now that the speculative provisions have been dealt with by the court, let him take the concrete case and do what he would do in his private business, have a decision of the court of last resort as to the validity of the proceedings. And I suggest to the minister that we should follow a course which is not unusual, which in fact we have frequently done in part if not in whole, that the expenses incident to the matter should be borne- with an understanding beforehand what they are to be-by the crown itself. In the meantime I suggest that the act itself should be continued just as though there had been no expression of opinion, which according to another decision of the supreme court is no better than that of the law officers of the crown themselves.

I would not feel competent to do so. But I should like to read to the committee the two sections which are concerned in the decision given. Section 5, subsection 4 reads:
Before any scheme is approved the governor in council shall be satisfied,
(a)	that the principal market for the natural product is outside the province of production; or
(b)	that some part of the product produced may be exported.
If that were the only statement in the act with regard to the matter I think there probably would be no doubt as to the view that should be held. But in section 2, paragraph (g) we find:
"Regulated product" means a natural product to which a scheme approved under this act relates, but does not include
(ii) in ease the said scheme relates only to the product marketed outside of the province of production, such product in so far as it is marketed within the province of production.
That is, it does not apply within the province?

Yes; there is an attempt made to make the situation appear as has been stated by the leader of the opposition, but apparently the court holds that there has been some interference with the marketing within the province itself, the local marketing. I do not intend to argue that point; the court has given its decision upon it. I would just say in regard to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) and supported by the leader of the opposition, that I am naturally not in a position to state exactly what the government will do in the circumstances set forth. I assume that a number of these acts which were submitted to the supreme court will be appealed to the privy council, and I think I can go so far as to state that the government will take exactly the same action in connection with this piece of legislation as they see fit to take in connection with the others.
They stand on a different basis.
One has been in operation.

The Minister of Justice will take this all under consideration, and we shall be advised in accordance with his views, also keeping before us, when we consider the matter, the expressions of opinion that have been given by both the hon. member for Yale and the leader of the opposition.

A short time ago when another item was under discussion the minister made a statement regarding the intention of the government not to continue the cheese bonus this year. That is going to be detrimental

to the dairy interests of Canada. The minister said at that time, and quite properly so, that the reason for giving the bonus for the sale of cheese last year was to increase the production of cheese in Canada and at the same time to curtail, if possible, the production of butter, the reason for that being that we were consuming all the butter we produced in Canada and for that reason the price was higher in Canada than it would have been had we been on an export basis. This was the reason which induced the former government, I believe, to give a bonus on cheese last year. But this is not the only reason. The minister also stated that the bonus last year had not been successful in achieving the purposes assigned. With that conclusion I am not prepared to agree. In the first place, for many years past the production of cheese in Canada had been gradually falling. In 1934 we manufactured about 99,000,000 pounds. In 1935 this had increased to 100,000,000 pounds, so that we had not only stopped the reduction by giving the bonus but already increased the production by a small amount.
A good deal has been said in this house about the importance of wheat growing as a branch of agriculture in Canada. I should like to point out how important the dairy industry is to this dominion. I took the trouble a short time ago to get some figures from the bureau of statistics regarding the value of the production of the different branches of agriculture in Canada. They gave me the figures for the six years 1939 to 1935 inclusive which I am going to read to the committee:
Live stock and animal products, $637,000,000.
Poultry and egg production, $327,000,000.
Fruit, $95,000,000.
Fodder crops, $1,057,000,000.
Wheat, $959,000,000.
Dairy products, $1,169,000,000.
Or over $200,000,000 more for dairy products than the value of wheat during those years. It seems to me, therefore, that while certain amounts have been spent to assist the wheat growers of the western provinces -and I have no fault whatever to find with that-the government might very well consider continuing this bonus for another year for the benefit of the dairy industry.
We produce in Canada annually some 16,000,000,000 pounds of milk. I should like to give the committee the percentages of that milk used in the manufacture of the different products into which that milk is manufactured and the different ways in which it is consumed. Cheese production took only 6-88 per cent of our milk production last year. Butter took 49-45 or approximately 50 per cent. One per cent is manufactured

Supply-M arine
into processed milk, such as condensed milk, powdered milk, et cetera; ice cream consumes only about one-half of one per cent of the milk that is produced, and some 42 per cent goes into fluid consumption.
A difficulty has arisen already this year which, it seems to me, is more or less alarming. I have before me the daily news letter sent out under the authority of the Minister of Agriculture. This issue dated June 15, states that the production of butter in Canada for the first five months of this year is ten per cent higher than it was for the first five months of last year. It seems to me, if that goes on for the year, that we shall be producing much more butter in Canada than we can possibly consume. If we get on an export basis I am afraid the price of butter will drop materially, and if the price of butter drops I am afraid the price of all other classes of dairy products in Canada will also drop accordingly.
I have only one further word to say. I do not need to go back over the ground and show that there has been a continual falling off in cheese production for the past number of years, or that there has been a gradual increase in butter production. The minister stated that another reason they were not giving the bonus this year is that there has been a certain amount of cheese sent to the United States since the inauguration of the present trade agreement. That is undoubtedly correct. But I do not think we can afford to sacrifice a market which we have had in Great Britain for years simply because we have entered into the American market for the time being. Canadian cheese enjoys a place of its own in the British market. For the past twenty or twenty-five years it has received a bonus of one, two and sometimes as high as four cents per pound in the British market. If we lose that market by failing to send our cheese to it and by failing to cater to it we would suffer a very serious loss indeed.
I have only one further observation and I shall have concluded. I should like to show how our cheese exports have fallen off. In 1927 we sent 136,000,000 pounds of cheese to the British market. By 1929 this had fallen to 112.000,000 pounds; in 1930, to 92,000,000 pounds. In 1934 it was 94,000,000 pounds:, and in 1935 it had dropped to 60,000,000 pounds. It seems to me that this is a serious situation. Only five per cent of all the dairy products we produce in Canada have to be exported, the other ninety-five per cent being consumed in Canada. If we are to hold our market in the British isles it seems to me that this is 12739-260
the only way in which it can be done, because the only way in which we can profitably export dairy products at this time is in the form of cheese. I am sorry the government has made this decision, and in conclusion my only observation would be that I hope by the time another year rolls around the dairy industry will not be suffering in the manner I am afraid that it will. If it is, I am sure that at that stage the government will do something about the matter.

speechtext: Yes.

The other evening when we were discussing it the minister made a statement which I thought at the time was not quite in accordance with the facts, not as a question of fact, but simply as a matter of professional opinion. He said:
As we improve the St. Lawrence river below, there is no question that when we take twelve

inches off the bottom, we take about five inches off the top. That goes on continuously.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Did I say five inches?

It was so reported, and I took the trouble to look the matter up, because before we entered into this contract we had a report prepared for the department by the joint board of engineers on the St. Lawrence waterway project. The report itself was prepared in November, 1926. That committee consisted of Messrs. D. W. McLachlan of the Department of Railways and Canals, Olivier
O.	Lefebvre, Chief Engineer of the Quebec Streams Commission; Brigadier General Charles Hamilton Mitchell; Major General Edgar Godwin, Chief of Engineers, in the United States; Colonel William Kelly, Corps of Engineers, United States; and Lieutenant Colonel George B. Pillsbury, Corps of Engineers, United States. We find the following at page 47, paragraph 211 of their report: Restoration of Navigable Depth
211. Channel below Montreal harbour-The navigable depth of the channel below Montreal harbour can be restored by dredging and an analysis of the gauge reports shows that the dredging heretofore done has lowered the level in Montreal harbour at the rate of 0T5 feet for each foot of navigable depth gained and has lowered the level of the river between Varennes and Quebec by an average of 0-06 for each foot of navigable depth gained.
According to this statement the dredging could have lowered the water level in the harbour of Montreal at the rate of 1% inches per foot of dredging, and three-quarters of an inch per foot of dredging in the main channel below Montreal.
I do not know whether the minister has had occasion to look up the interim report of March 4, 1935, but the Interdepartmental Montreal and Ship Channel Water Level Board state on pages 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8, paragraphs 8 to 22, the cause of low water conditions. I shall1 not go into the matter at length, but I believe the minister was inaccurately reported, because these are the words used by the board:
A loss of 1-75 feet due to dredging of deeper and wider channel below the upper harbour; of this amount about 0-80 feet is due to dredging between the upper and the lower harbour.
Again, at paragraph 21, the board states:
The above table 5 shows a drop of 1-70 feet in water level in Montreal upper harbour due to enlargements and obstructions in channel of Montreal and in the river below. Of this amount, 1T0 feet may be ascribed to work done by the harbour commissioners of Montreal and 0-60 may be ascribed to work done in the ship channel below.
These two statements really mean that the dredging in the main channel has been responsible for a drop of 0-80 feet or 0-60

feet. We must remember that the drop in the level due to dredging is greater at a lower level of water. Without going into the matter at length I think it is sufficient to say that the drop in depth caused by dredging depends upon the distribution of the area of water, and under present conditions it would appear that the loss cannot be greater than, say a little over three-quarters of an inch per foot. This report that we had before us at the time we were entering into this agreement was another departmental report supplementing the report of 1926 to which I have made reference. I had notes prepared covering the whole situation, but I desire only to correct that, because if the statement made by the minister were accurate we have been greatly misled in dealing with the matter, and I wanted to verify it by reference to the original of the report of 1935, supplementing the report of 1926, to ascertain that the figures upon which we relied were at least those that were contained in the report. I think it may be fairly said that the dredging reduces the depth in the harbour approximately three-quarters of an inch per foot.

To reimburse Peter R. Jack and Chas. A. Aekhurst, one-time harbour commissioners at Halifax, for expenses incurred by them in connection with the inquiry into the administration of the Halifax harbour commission in 1930, $3,855.10.

I should like an explanation from the minister as to why an attempt should be made to reimburse these two gentlemen for expenses incurred by them in connection with this inquiry. Documents brought down by the minister disclosed-is it too strong to say?- very discreditable action on the part of that commission. The full report of the commissioner could not be made on account of his death. But it seems to me novel and unprecedented to propose a vote to pay for the legal expenses incurred by these two gentlemen. I should like to know why that proposal is made.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
These two gentlemen were appointed by the government to conduct a government service at Halifax. Their services were dispensed with, charges of improper conduct were brought, and a judge was appointed to investigate. These men were under obligation, I think, to the government to defend the position they had taken. They hired counsel to do so. Before doing so they wrote to the

Supply-M iscellaneous
Department of Marine and asked for counsel to be appointed by the department. The deputy minister of the department, whose letter we have on file, wrote them that consideration would be given to the cost of counsel. The case was tried.
If the minister has the letter, will he read just what the deputy minister said? That may be very important from our standpoint.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Yes. This is a letter to the then Deputy Minister of Marine, Mr. Alex. Johnston, under date of November 13, 1930:
Mr. Charles W. Ackhurst, one of the other commissioners, as well as myself have engaged the services of Mr. L. A. Lovett, K.C., and I wish to take this opportunity of drawing this matter to your attention and to ask that you arrange to defray the expenses of our counsel and any other expenses that we shall be subject to in connection with this inquiry.
To this Mr. Johnston made reply on November 17, 1930, as follows:
Just a line to acknowledge receipt of yours of the 13th instant and to say that the representations contained therein will in due course be submitted for consideration.
The inquiry proceeded, and I understand that complete evidence was taken. I have not personally read all the evidence, but I asked one of our officers to read it and to draw to my attention anything that he thought was pertinent as reflecting on the actions of the commissioners. The judge conducting the case, when he was about to prepare his report, died,. No other judge was assigned to complete the work, and these two men, who had been public servants, were left in the position of having been accused and of being unable either to have themselves acquitted or proven guilty. I think this is a very unfortunate position. I must say that in reading the evidence I could find nothing which seemed in any way to justify the charges. It seemed to me that it was in view of the public service of these men that they were placed in that position.' They being accused of criminal actions, and being proven neither guilty nor innocent, it seemed to me that the least the government could do was to, reimburse them for their out of pocket expense for legal assistance.

It is a very serious
matter to create a precedent of this kind. I am not going to discuss the matter now, but a perusal of the evidence leaves certain convictions in one's mind. I believe the minister is wrong in saying that any criminal proceedings were suggested. But compare this treatment with that of the man whom I mentioned this morning! Just compare 12739-2601
what is being done for these men at Halifax with the treatment accorded to the man whom the former Secretary of State discussed in this house, who lost his job, against whom not a single word of evidence was adduced, and who still alleges that there never was any evidence which could be produced against him! Certainly that cannot be said in connection with this Halifax matter. But this other poor unfortunate, unimportant in the world, not occupying a position like that of a harbour commissioner, having no redress and no ability to hire lawyers, much less to write letters asking the department to be reimbursed for any expenditure, has nothing done for him. We are creating a precedent which may be very useful with respect to such unfortunates as I referred to this morning, and I only hope that the same measure of generosity will be extended to those who are less vocal, less important, and who cannot make the same contribution to the well-being of political parties that the commissioners of Halifax harbour could do. I cannot but think that this is a precedent which will have far-reaching consequences. The death of the judge was not the only difficulty; it had the effect of terminating the whole inquiry and necessitating a new inquiry being carried on by a new judge, and some of the evidence was no longer available, and would have to be heard over again by whoever was appointed. I was not in the country when the commission was appointed; I know nothing about the matter beyond reading the testimony that was brought down, but certainly the minister would find it difficult to say that he had read the evidence and was satisfied there was no cause for just complaint. However, I remember this one circumstance. Before the contract was made at all, certain steps were taken by the commissioners which it would be difficult to justify in dealing with a transaction of that kind. It will be recalled that the final contract in connection with the matter, which involved very heavy expenditures being made by this dominion,, was executed between the defeat of the government and the coming into office of its successors. That is true at least in connection with part; I cannot say that it is true with respect to the whole. I point out to the minister that the precedent is very far-reaching and enables me to assert with some measure of authority the right of those to whom I referred this morning to receive similar treatment from the government of the day.

I must say to my hon.
friend that it is true that the position of assistant electoral officer has not been filled for a number of years, but the salary has been voted every year. I do not know what has been the experience of my hon. friend, but even when I was in office previously the chief electoral officer always pleaded that it was not wise to leave that office without an assistant.
Oh, oh.

My hon. friends may smile, but I think that is right. I am going to remind my hon. friend that when he appointed a dominion franchise commissioner he also appointed an assistant, and this is in exactly the same position. It is a very small office, consisting of Mr. Castonguay and two or three minor clerks, and if Mr. Castonguay goes away for a day or so the office is practically left alone. The fact is that not only were we right in appointing Mr. Stewart to that position but that an appointment should have been made some time ago. Now that we are going to revise the electoral law I think it is very wise to have assistants for both the franchise and electoral officers, to be trained as such under the main officers.
All I can say is that when I went into office in 1930 the office of assistant had not been filled for some years.
I think both parties are to blame.

The chief electoral officer then had the duties of both electoral officer and franchise commissioner. Early in the first

Supply-State
year some question arose as to the duties of Mr. Castonguay's office, and I called Mr. Castonguay to my office and asked as to the need of appointing such an assistant. He told me it would1 be utterly indefensible for the government to appoint an assistant, because during a great part of the time he had very little to do. He said that he did not need an assistant, and that if his recommendation was required with regard to the appointment he certainly would not give it. That was the gist of his conversation with me. Subsequently the work of the office was divided, and at least half the work of the chief electoral officer was given to the franchise commissioner. Before the general election I suppose I must have had a score of applications for the appointment of somebody as assistant in this office. I again called Mr. Castonguay to my office and I have a very clear recollection concerning the interview. He stated that the appointment of an assistant was not necessary, and that if it depended upon his recommendation he certainly would not recommend it. I so advised my colleagues, and no appointment was made. In fact a suggestion had been made in regard to the appointment of a particular individual, and I may not reveal what took place at a certain place but I shall say that I advised all my colleagues that I would not support that waste of money.

I suppose there never was a greater piece of political jobbery in this country than the appointment of this man to this job. What the former Secretary of State has said I desire to support, because not merely by scores but by more than that people were asking for the position. It was too late to take steps to abolish it; if it had been abolished there would have been less trouble. The present government when in office from 1921 to 1930 did not fill the position. The commissioner then had the duties of both offices. In 1925-26 the position was not filled. When the general election of 1930 came on it was not filled. During the five intervening years it was not filled. In 1935 before the general election it was not filled. But now this S3,000 job has been filled by the appointment of the son of the president of the Liberal association in Ottawa, after the position had remained vacant all these years and after a general election, when the duties, according to the chief electoral officer, are very light indeed. In fact, it was because of the representations made by the then Secretary of State to his colleagues and after the closest inquiry, and after he had communicated to us the sense of what he has now said, that it was quite clear that no appointment could or
should be made. This is another illustration of what my hon. friends may call the practice of economy.

I should not like to seem discourteous in not replying. I can only say what I said before, that in both these small offices we thought it was proper to have a chief officer and an assistant. I do not doubt for a moment that the statements made by the former Secretary of State are accurate, but I shall say on my personal word that Mr. Castonguay came to my office and pleaded with me more than once that we fill this job.

On a former occasion when these estimates were before the committee I expressed the desire to make a lengthy statement, but I shall restrict my observations considerably; if hon. members will permit me I shall make only a short statement.
My contention is, first, that the passing of certain orders in council prohibiting imports from Italy into Canada and certain exports from Canada to Italy were passed without proper authority; and second, that the agreement made with respect to the imposition of sanctions at Geneva was not made through an organ of the League of Nations, and that the suggestion that the League of Nations was recommending the imposition of sanctions, as a league, is not in accordance with the facts; and third, that the action with regard to sanctions is a repudiation of the pledges made to this parliament by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) on a previous occasion, and not in accordance with a resolution introduced by the Prime Minister and passed unanimously by parliament in June, 1926.
I do not intend to enter upon a full discussion of the matters, but I should like to refer to them in order that they might be considered before further sanctions are imposed or further action taken, so that they may be considered in another light by the Prime Minister and his advisers.
On October 31, 1935, an order in council,
P.C. 3461 was passed by His Excellency the Governor in Council, prohibiting the exportation, reexportation or transit to Italy or to any Italian possession of the arms, munitions and implements of war enumerated in a list attached thereto, and it was ordered that a proclamation to that effect be issued forthwith and published in The Canada Gazette.
That order in council was passed under the authority of section 290 of the Customs Act and was, in my opinion, a valid and effective exercise of a power conferred on the executive by legislation of parliament.
On November 15. 1935, an order in council, P.C. 3594 was passed by His Excellency the Governor in Council, prohibiting by article 1, imports from Italy into Canada; and by article 2, certain exports from Canada to Italy; and by article 3, prohibiting any person in Canada from making, contributing to, participating in or assisting in the making of any loan to or for the benefit of,-
(1)	The government of any Italian territory, that is to say, the kingdom of Italy and the colonies or dependencies thereof and any territory in the effective military occupation of Italy;
(2)	Any person, not being a body corporate, of whatever nationality resident in any such territory;-
A most extraordinary thing.
-or (3) Any person wherever resident being a body corporate incorporated under the law of any such territory.
A subsequent amendment of the same order provides that giving a guarantee or becoming party to a bill of exchange, or buying a bill of exchange, or giving credit in any form shall be deemed for the purposes of this article to be making a loan.
This order in council is entitled the Treaty of Peace (Covenant of the League of Nations) Order, 1935. But it was not made in pursuance of any obligations which Canada had as a member of the League of Nations, and it is a misnomer to call it a covenant of the League of Nations order.
The Customs Act in section 290, provides:
290. The governor in council may, from time to time, prohibit the exportation or the carrying coastwise or by inland navigation, of arms, ammunition and gunpowder, military and naval stores, and any articles which the governor in council deems capable of being converted into or made useful in increasing the quantity of military or naval stores, provisions or any sort of victual which may be used as food by man.
In so far as the order in council of November 15, 1935, P.C. 3594, prohibits exports from Canada within the terms of section 290 of the Customs Act, it was passed with the authority of parliament, but, in so far as the said order in council prohibits either exports or imports which are not authorized by the Customs Act,

I respectfully submit that the said order in council was passed without express parliamentary authority and is of doubtful validity.
Whence did the government assume that the extraordinary powers were derived which purport to be exercised in the order in council of November 15, 1935? The order recites that it is made under the provisions of the Treaties of Peace Act, 1919, but certainly no member of the House of Commons or of the Senate of Canada in 1919 conceived that the Treaties of Peace Act, 1919, would be construed, in 1935, to authorize the government of Canada, without the consent of parliament, that is, without the consent of both the Commons and the Senate of Canada, to prohibit all trade, all financial and business dealings between residents of Canada, and all those resident in Italy or in Italian territories, even though they be British or Canadian nationals temporarily resident there.
Moreover, if the government of Canada was authorized by that act of 1919 to impose economic sanctions against Italy or against any other nation, without consulting parliament, then the same act of 1919 authorized the government of Canada, without consulting parliament, to impose military and naval sanctions as suggested by the terms of the covenant of the League of Nations and to enter upon active warfare against any recalcitrant member of the League of Nations, Italy or any other nation, then or at a future date. When the parliament of Canada had the Treaties of Peace Act, 1919, under consideration, the Hon. W. S. Fielding, I well remember, inquired of the government of the day whether that involved the carrying out of the terms of the covenant. The question was first put, would it authorize the appointment of a delegate to Geneva in order that organization might be made under the league covenant, and the answer was a specific no, given by the Minister of Justice of the day, although later he did modify to a certain extent that emphatic no by saying that it might authorize the government to send a delegate to Geneva for the purposes mentioned.
The parliament of New Zealand, on November 24 last, enacted The League of Nations (Enforcement in New Zealand) Act, 1935. This special act authorized economic sanctions only, and provides that naval or military sanctions would require further special authorization by parliament. The New Zealand act empowers the governor general by order in council to make regulations enabling the dominion to fulfil its obligations under article 16 of the League of Nations to enforce economic sanctions, but it requires that

all such regulations shall be laid before parliament within twenty days after the making thereof if parliament is then in session, and if not, then within twenty days after the commencement of the next ensuing session. This New Zealand act also provides that the regulations are to lapse on the expiration of two months after they have been so laid before parliament except so far as they are expressly validated or confirmed by an act of parliament. By that New Zealand legislation the rights of parliament are strictly preserved.
Again, the parliament of Australia, when called upon to deal with the matter of sanctions, passed an act relating to the application of sanctions against Italy for the purpose of implementing the proposals of the coordination committee of eighteen.
On November 7 last the Dail of the Irish Free State also enacted a special statute entitled the League of Nations (Obligations of Membership) Act for the same purpose.
No session of the parliament of Canada was convened to consider this matter, and if the government of Canada had authority under the Treaties of Peace Act, 1919, to enter upon and' prescribe economic sanctions, it had exactly the same authority to provide for naval and military as well as economic warfare against Italy. The Treaties of Peace Act, 1919, which is chapter 30 of the acts of parliament for that year, recites that on behalf ^ of the allied and associated powers treaties of peace had been signed with Germany and Austria, and then provides:
(1) The governor in council may make such appointments, establish such offices, make such orders in council, and do such things as appear to him to be necessary for carrying out the said treaties, and for giving effect to any of the provisions of the said treaties.
Did any mortal man in parliament or outside parliament in Canada conceive at that time, under that clause, which was intended and stated to be intended to wind up the matters relating to war under the war measures acts, and to adjust the conditions in Canada resulting from the war, that it was the intention that ten or twenty or one hundred years thereafter the government of the day would be authorized by such general terms to impose sanctions and to precipitate a state of war between this country and any other nation that was a party to the covenant?
Discussions in the commons in 1919 were participated in, if I remember correctly, by the Minister of Justice of this day. I believe that the Minister of Pensions was then in parliament, and that he asked very pertinent questions with regard to the purpose and in-
