tent of that act, and it was explained that it would merely authorize the government to adjust financial and other matters such as indemnities, reparations and the like, arising out of the war, and then awaiting adjustment and settlement. It was never suggested to parliament that for a decade or a century in the future that act would authorize the government of the day by order in council to exercise the powers and legislative functions of parliament in relation to all matters arising out of the operation under the covenant of the League of Nations.
When the covenant of the League of Nations was under discussion in the parliament and press of this country in 1919, special emphasis was laid upon the last two paragraphs of article 4 and the first paragraph of article 5 of the covenant. It was then explained and contended by those then advocating the ratification of the covenant, that in respect of any prospective decision of the council of the league that might specially affect the interests of any member of the league which was not represented on the council, such a member would be invited to send a representative to sit as a member of council and to vote in respect of that decision, and that, as such decision must be unanimous, Canada, even as such member pro tempore, would have the power to veto any proposed decision specially affecting Canada's interests. That was so stated to be the purpose and intent of the provision. This contention was based on the provisions of articles 4 and 5 of the covenant, which read as follows:
Article 4. Any member of the league not represented on the council shall be invited to send a representative to sit as a member at any meeting of the council during the consideration of matters specially affecting the interests of that member of the league.
Article 5. At meetings of the council, each member of the league represented on the council shall have one vote, and may have not more than one representative.... _
Except where otherwise expressly provided in this covenant or by the terms of the present treaty, decisions at any meeting of the assembly or of the council shall require the agreement of all the members of the league represented at the meeting.
It was impossible to reach within the terms of the covenant any agreement between all the nations represented on the League of Nations to enter upon any campaign of sanctions against Italy. There were, and it was openly stated that there were, two or three who were recalcitrant and would not endorse a unanimous resolution to enforce sanctions against Italy. But those who were anxious to impose sanctions against Italy very adroitly arranged that, outside the league assembly, outside the organs of the league, representatives of the governments might be convened and a new organ created of those members who were agreeable to and accepted the proposal to impose effective sanctions against Italy. We saw it stated in the press from one end to the other of this country and in other countries as well that this committee which was so constituted was not a league organ but was created outside the league, and was not merely carrying out the terms of the covenant of the league. In my opinion it was a mere pretence to assume that the character and dignity of the league would cover such action as might be agreed upon independently by certain members of the league in the adoption and enforcement of sanctions against Italy.
Hon. members are aware that after full discussion in the assembly of the league and its committees in the years 1921, 1923, 1924 and 1925, various proposals were presented for amendments to sections 10 and 16 of the covenant of the league, which could only be invoked by such unanimous action as I have stated. In order to provide uniform methods whereby military and naval sanctions might be adopted and enforced, a treaty of mutual assistance was drafted at Geneva in 1923 and reported for the favourable consideration of members of the league. That draft treaty provided in detail for the coordination of all measures for the enforcement of military and economic sanctions against a recalcitrant member of the league. That draft treaty was intended to define and supplement the existing obligations contained in article 16, and to obviate the necessity of unanimous agreement for the adoption and enforcement of sanctions.
The Prime Minister of that day, who is the Prime Minister of to-day, in a memorandum to the League of Nations, signed by himself on behalf of Canada, declined to approve the proposed treaty of mutual assistance on the ground that Canada would not agree "to transfer the right to decide upon the scope of the action Canada should take from the Canadian parliament to the council of the League of Nations." The letter of the present Prime Minister rejecting, on behalf of Canada, the proposed treaty of mutual assistance was dated July 9, 1924, and will be found in the records of the assembly of the League of Nations for 1924, at page 146. This letter reads in part as follows:
Canada has already indicated disapproval of the interpretation of the terms of article 10 of the covenant as implying an obligation upon her to intervene actively under that article. The proposed treaty creates an obligation wider in its extent and more precise in its implications than any which article 10 could be interpreted as imposing, and it proposes, moreover, to transfer the right to decide upon the scope of the action Canada should take from the

There was then no doubt in the mind of the present Prime Minister that the imposition of economic or military sanctions by Canada against any recalcitrant member of the league must first be specially authorized by the parliament of Canada. At that time public discussion of the liability of members of the league in regard to the enforcement of military and economic sanctions against an aggressor state became very lively indeed. The proposed treaty of mutual assistance in the carrying into effect of these sanctions failed to obtain general support and was never brought into force. Not only did Canada not accept it, but she made independent representations to Great Britain with respect to it and Great Britain failed to accept it as well.
As a result of these discussions, the matter was again brought up at the imperial conference which met at London in 1926. That imperial conference adopted a resolution recommending that a certain procedure should be observed in the negotiation, signature and ratification of international treaties and conventions. On his return to Canada, the Prime Minister of that day expressed himself as not being satisfied with the form of the resolution proposed and approved at that imperial conference of 1926. On June 21. 1926, as reported on page 4758 of Hansard of that year, the Prime Minister of that day, the right hon. gentleman who is Prime Minister to-day, submitted this resolution of the imperial conference for the approval of the House of Commons, but he attached to the imperial conference proposal a very significant clause. The Prime Minister's resolution, after citing the procedure mentioned, proceeds as follows to indicate that independent action should be taken by Canada:
This house approves of the procedure proposed for the negotiation, signature, and ratification of treaties and conventions, and advises further that before His Majesty's Canadian 
ministers advise ratification of a treaty or convention affecting Canada, or signify acceptance of any treaty, convention or agreement involving military or economic sanctions, the approval of the parliament of Canada should be secured.
At that time I sat as a member of His Majesty's loyal opposition and the Conservative members of that opposition asked me to discuss in the house the terms of that resolution. During his remarks on that occasion, the Prime Minister said, as reported on page 4756 of Hansard:
We declare that in regard to the ratification of_ treaties, conventions or agreements involving military or economic sanctions we stand first, last and always for approval in the first instance by the parliament of Canada.
In reply to a question put by myself, the Prime Minister said, as reported on page 4768 of Hansard:
What I wish to make clear, however, was that all treaties or conventions involving military or_ economic sanctions must come before parliament, and where military or economic sanctions were involved I wished to make the terms broad enough to include agreements, so that in referring to treaties or agreements of any kind we should not have a difference over the mere use of words.
In commenting upon this, the former member for Labelle, Mr. Bourassa, gave the following interpretation, to which no member of the government or any member of the house dissented at the time:
The government invites the cooperation of parliament and declaration by parliament that no treaty, convention or agreement, whether Canada is mentioned or not, but involving military or economic sanctions, shall be accepted by the government of Canada without the approval of parliament.
Representing for the day His Majesty's opposition, I commended highly the stand taken by the Prime Minister. The result was that the resolution which I have mentioned passed this house unanimously.
Therefore I was somewhat surprised on February 11 last, with respect to the statement of the Prime Minister regarding the sanctions enforced against Italy by Canada, by orders in council to which I have called attention, and without parliament being called together, without the opinion of parliament being taken, without that confirmation of the action of the government which was necessary if the pledge given to parliament and the resolution adopted by parliament were to be carried into effect, as understood at the time, in 1926-I was somewhat surprised, I say, at the statement of the Prime Minister on that date:
On October 29th I issued a statement to the effect that Canada would apply these sanctions. Sanctions were enforced by Canada on the

In discussing the matter at the opening of the session a question was put in reply to which the present Prime Minister said, as reported at page 94 of Hansard of the present session:
May I say to my right hon. friend, because I understand his difficulty in appreciating the situation, that the committee of coordination at Geneva was not a League of Nations committee in the sense in which I have no doubt he regards it. It was not a committee of the assembly nor a committee of the council. It was a committee of representatives of different countries represented at Geneva who took under review the question of deciding what particular sanctions the different countries that were representatives of the league would agree upon. This committee set up a further committee of eighteen.

It was perfectly clear, and admitted, that the ordinary procedure under which unanimity would be required in the council and in the assembly in order to carry out, under the League of Nations, the proposed economic war against Italy by imposing sanctions, was impossible of achievement; and therefore, at a plenary meeting of the League of Nations held on October 10, 1935, the president made a statement which, in the official report of that plenary meeting of the assembly, reads as follows:
The president said that the general committee had considered, with a view to laying suggestions before the assembly, what arrangements might be suggested for the constitution of the organ of coordination. The delegation of Italy, vice-president of the assembly, sitting in that capacity in the general committee, had stated, at the opening of the meeting, whilst repeating his earlier reservations, that le would abstain from taking part in the leliberations.
Then he proceeds:
He would add that the organ which the members of the league were invited to constitute was not an organ of the assembly or of the council. It would be a kind of conference of members meeting to consult together with a view to applying the provisions of article 16.
That was indeed a very suave and tactful way of stating that a new international agreement was proposed to be framed by which the nations which accepted it would commit themselves to the imposition of economic or military sanctions against Italy. It was a coordinating committee. It was not deemed to be an organ of the council or an organ of the assembly of the league. It was merely a meeting of representatives of member states to frame a new agreement among themselves as to the enforcement of sanctions against Italy. At page 267 of the Journal the Baron Aloisi of Italy said:
The proposed committee could not therefore be regarded as in any way an organ of the league. As the president himself had explained, it was only a conference of certain states consulting together on the steps which they would agree to take on their own responsibility.
I am anxious to conclude and shall go through my notes as rapidly as possible. At page 267 of the Journal the president replied :
No body of the league had the power to decide compulsorily for all members that one of them had committed a breach of the covenant.

Then he went on to say:
Having replied to the first observation of the delegate of Italy, he would admit that the delegate of Italy was right in respect of the doubts expressed regarding a vote on the resolution if the text before the assembly was to be regarded as a formal resolution of the assembly. In that case the question of unanimity or voting by a majority would arise. He had felt bound to state at once that, in the present instance, the assembly was not asked to consider a resolution in the strict sense of the word but an invitation addressed by the assembly to the states members.
The original draft used the word "invites'' and he suggested that it should be replaced by "recommends" because there was no authority on the part of the assembly to invite such a conference. Then, without going fully into the matter, this coordination committee set up a committee of eighteen, consisting of the representatives of eighteen states. When this committee met Mr. Coulondre, the French representative-and I know Mr. Coulondre as one of the most astute officials on the permanent staff of the French foreign office- said:
The committee of eighteen, an offshoot of the coordination committee, was a conference of sovereign states-
And, as a conference of sovereign states it sought to reach an agreement between the several states respecting the enforcement of economic sanctions. Later the matter was dealt with. At this stage I do not intend to deal with the various discussions whereby Canada was represented on this coordination committee, or with the proposal of Doctor Riddell, as the representative of the sovereign state of Canada, or with the fact that the various representatives in discussing that proposition referred to it, as the official report shows, as the Canadian proposition.

The committee of eighteen reported back to the coordination committee and the coordination committee adopted the report. So Canada entered into a new formal agreement with regard to the imposition of sanctions, an agreement which was not covered by the terms of the covenant and which was made through an organ, so-called, outside the council and the assembly.
I suggest that when the Prime Minister, as Minister of External Affairs, proposed the orders in council adopting and imposing sanctions, which have been laid upon the table of the house, he certainly had forgotten altogether the resolution of this house, introduced iby himself, under which no agreement of any kind would be made thereafter-and that was in June, 1926-with regard to the imposition of economic or military sanctions without parliament being convened and confirming that agreement. I think, first, that except by resorting possibly to the peace, order and good government clause of certain then existing statutes, to which the Prime Minister would not resort under any circumstances on that date but to which he has resorted on several occasions since, there was no statutory or moral right or authority on the part of the government to adopt and impose the sanctions which I have mentioned, other than the embargo on the export of arms.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sure my hon. friend the member for St. Lawrence-St. George does not regret more than I do that at this stage of the session and at this hour of a closing day it is not possible to go fully into the all important matters he has been discussing. What my hon. friend has said does bring out very clearly how involved with respect to the matter of sanctions the whole question of procedure at Geneva has been and also the necessity of careful revision of some features of the covenant of the league and the obligations assumed thereunder. That revision may be expected to take place this fall. I believe that what my hon. friend has put on the record this evening will be of assistance not only to our own government but to other governments as well in reviewing the entire situation.
As I understand my hon. friend's point of attack, it is mainly that the present administration imposed sanctions by order in council when a resolution had passed this house some years ago to the effect that the government should not in future enter into agreements to impose sanctions without the approval of parliament in the first instance. May I say
in just a word that I had not forgotten the resolution of 1926. In fact it was very much in my mind at the time the government had to deal with this question. But it was perfectly clear to me then as it is now that the resolution related, not to treaties and agreements that had been entered into in the past, but to treaties and agreements which might be entered into thereafter. We were not entering into a new treaty; we were taking action under a treaty which had been in existence for some years. My hon. friend takes exception to our having acted under that treaty. May I say that if our course is to be condemned in that particular the British government itself must also be condemned, because it adopted an identical course, it proceeded under precisely the same treaty. The action taken by the British government in passing the orders in council imposing sanctions was taken under the Treaty of Peace Act, 1919 the action of the British government was taken before the Canadian government took the action it did.
May I point out further that the British government took the action it did by order in council while its parliament was in session. In the case of the other dominions I think most of their parliaments were in session at the time. We were faced with a situation which was one of great reality. It required to be viewed in a realistic manner. The problem with respect to the imposition of sanctions for the most part had presented itself before this administration came into office. To a certain extent it might be said that our hands were tied with respect to the action it would be possible to take. I prefer to say that we had to consider very carefully how parliament would view our action in imposing sanctions by order in council. Considering all the circumstances we felt that, having regard to the situation itself, to the position of hon. gentlemen opposite when they themselves were in office and the support which we as an administration had received from the country and would have in this parliament there was little doubt that, as soon as parliament did assemble, our actions would receive the support of hon. members on all sides. I think we were fully justified in making that assumption and acting in the light of it. The fact that this is the first time this question has been raised in parliament since parliament assembled some five months ago is the best evidence that the administration has a right to feel that it did act wisely and wholly in accordance with the wishes of hon. members of the House of Commons in this matter.
I do not wish to take up time, but I think it is important to make clear the following

The committee recommended that the first recommendation should be put into force forthwith. All of that was done while hon. gentlemen opposite were in office, while my right hon. friend the present leader of the opposition was Prime Minister. All that had taken place before the present government assumed office at all. We came into office on October 23. We then had to consider whether we should immediately call parliament before imposing sanctions. Parliament could not have been brought together for at least another six weeks. What position would Canada have been in before the rest of the world had we called parliament together to consider what action should be taken on sanctions, and had waited six weeks or more before these sanctions were imposed, when it was recommended at Geneva by the powers represented there that sanctions, to be of value, should be imposed with as little delay as possible; forthwith, in fact? I have mentioned that the recommendation with respect to the prohibition of export of arms urged that the prohibition should be imposed forthwith. That was done by Canada on October 31, P.C. 3461, under section 290 of the Customs Act. I think my 'hon. friend will agree that under the Customs Act we had authority to do that. With respect to the second recommendation, the prohibition of loans and credits, on October 14 the committee-

May I point out another circumstance which I suggest ought to be considered. The government had to consider the entire situation and ask itself what would be the result of bringing parliament together some six weeks later, the first session after a general election. One measure which we felt to be vital to the success of trade in Canada was if possible, a reciprocal agreement with the United States. Certainly no reciprocal agreement with that country could have been negotiated during that period of time had the government been obliged to take immediate steps to bring parliament into session. We would have lost all opportunity of getting that measure underway or securing it at all. A new government taking office after a general election, and after a previous government has held office for more than five years, is faced with a multitude of problems. To have immediately brought parliament together to deal with the question of sanctions would have meant that, so far as the business of the session was concerned, it would have been practically impossible to have had legislation in readiness for hon. members. Moreover, a wholly erroneous impression of the European situation might thereby have been created. If there had been the slightest probability that there would have been objection to not bringing hon. members together for the purpose of obtaining their consent before sanctions were imposed, I say that, notwithstanding all the difficulties there might have been, parliament would have been summoned for that purpose. But we believed-and I think this session has confirmed the wisdom of our decision-that, when they assembled, hon. members would view this matter in the light of all the circumstances, with which the government was faced, and would feel that the government had acted in a way which was most in accordance with their wishes and most in accordance with the will of the Canadian people.
I should like to put before the committee the position in which the country would 12739-261
have been if we had waited before imposing sanctions until parliament could assemble. This dominion would have been responsible for not having agreed to impose sanctions at a time when practically all other parts of the British empire and other countries members of the league had imposed them. We would have been open to criticism on this score. I think my right hon. friend, had he been in office, would have found, just as we found, ample precedent and authority in the example of the British government with respect to imposing sanctions by order in council, under the act to which I have referred.
I say all this without in any way wishing to indicate that I do not think the hon. member was quite within his rights in bringing up the matter and speaking as he did and, in fact, criticizing the government as he did. I fully expected that criticism would be made. I can only thank the hon. member for the considerate manner in which he has spoken, and I thank the house as well for not having found it necessary to seek to bring any criticism on this score until the last hours in the last day of the session.

With respect to New Zealand may I say that that country convened a meeting of its parliament and passed the League of Nations Enforcement in New Zealand Act, 1935, on November 24. They delayed until after November 24 to put their order in council into effect. They also provided that within twenty-eight days after the commencement of the next ensuing session, the one after the special session, the regulations would lapse unless parliament should ratify them within twenty-eight days after the next ensuing session. What the Prime Minister has said has some force. It has this force: That a government having serious problems to face must at times face them by taking action for which there may be no clear statutory authority at the time, feeling confident that when parliament meets it will by act of parliament ratify and confirm the action the government has taken. That has to be done frequently, in times of emergency. But when I raised the question at the beginning of the session and suggested an early discussion the Prime Minister asked to have it postponed to a later date, and suggested that at such later date the matter would be brought up.
Some hon. members on this side of the house were waiting until the last bill was brought down expecting that the government would bring down a bill and ask the house to ratify and confirm the action it had taken

speechtext:
I agree with my hon. friend when he says that the action of the government at this time should not be regarded as a precedent. I feel as strongly as he does that parliament should, in all of these matters, have its voice heard before the country is committed to anything that may involve us in a war.
I make no apology, however, for not having invited a debate on this subject at an earlier stage of the session. There again, what my hon. friend has just said about a government facing actual situations and deciding its course in the light of them, has its force. I believe I can say now, in the light of what has been said by the Prime Minister of Great Britain as to the significance which the imposition of further sanctions upon Italy would have, that there was the possibility of a debate in this house arousing adverse comment and possibly more in the way of misunderstanding in Europe. That would not have helped the situation there. After all, while the situation in Europe is of great concern to all the people in Canada, it is of infinitely greater concern to the people of European countries. They, I believe, were entitled to first consideration. I believe this parliament has contributed to the solution of that situation, in so far as there has thus far been a solution, much more effectively by its silence, up to the present-so far as it has been silent-than it would have contributed by any prolonged discussion.

I am not going to enter into a lengthy speech at this hour of the night, but I am as anxious as the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) or any other hon. member to speak on this subject. I do not agree with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in his last observation that anything which would be said in this parliament regarding Canada's foreign policy or her position in respect to

sanctions, or on any other question, would be as upsetting as was feared.

I disagree with the Prime Minister. I do not think a discussion in this house would have been upsetting, and I think it is a left-over of colonialism that we cannot discuss in the House of Commons matters which are freely discussed in the British house.

speechtext: Again may I say to my hon. friend that I pointed out in this house that anyone who wished to bring up the subject could bring it up at any time we were going into committee of supply, but that he must take the responsibility for bringing it up, rather than that the government should take responsibility for introducing the discussion. We spent one month debating the trade agreement between Canada and the United States, which could not be in any way changed. A month is a long time, and I think most of the debate was useless.

In theory that is true. In practice the house would approve it when the government approves it, because the government in this instance is almost the house. But we did take a month on the trade agreement between Canada and the United

States; we were promised by the Prime Minister himself a day to discuss Canada's foreign policy or external affairs, and we did not get anything like a day. All we got before six o'clock was a very interesting statement by the Prime Minister, for which I thank him. and in which he went further in the direction of my thinking than I expected he would go. It was a very interesting statement. It was one that touched many angles of the problem and one that gave me a desire to discuss it. But after the Prime Minister had finished his statement at six o'clock there were just two hours left, so that the day that we were to have for external affairs boiled down to just two hours. For this reason I protest. It is impossible to go on at this time; no one feels like it and the committee is not in a mood for it. But at another session the importance of Canada's external or foreign policy should be recognized by allowing plenty of time for discussion. We spend days and weeks in fairly futile talk, and why could we not have a debate on Canada's foreign policy? It seems hard to find a real reason. In the Prime Minister's speech, which I enjoyed, the other day, in the speech made by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), to a degree in the speeches made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodswort'h) and by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), one could see a lack of clearness of thinking which I have and which we all have. That is, Canada is only feeling its way to a much more distinctively Canadian foreign policy than we have ever had before.
Three lines of thought showed very distinctly in at any rate three of those speeches: the collectivist or league line of thinking, which in theory we all once subscribed to, the imperialistic line of thinking, and last, the more isolationist or North American way of thinking. I am not clear and I do not believe any other hon. member is very clear about what he or she thinks Canada should do, other than we feel that Canada's foreign policy should be determined by Canada's interests and should not be too closely allied either with empire policy, or with league policy unless league policy is materially changed from what it is at the moment. I am not going on, because it is useless to do so. But I repeat that at another session not only one day but several days should be available so that the House of Commons may in some degree clarify its thinking on this subject, which is certainly a very important one, and much more important than, shall we say, the trade agreement with the United States, on which we spent a very long time.

I had intended to make an appeal to the government still further to enlarge the amount of the subventions to be voted, on the ground that I believe this would be probably one of the most productive investments we could make in the way of solving our unemployment problem. I have now made up my mind, however, that instead of going into the matter as fully as I had intended I shall submit a statement to the government in writing, because the argument I intended to present to-night would have had for its purpose only to ask the government to look into the question of subventions more fully during the recess in the hope that a permanent policy might be evolved for submission to parliament at the next session.
The other matter I had in mind has to do with the question of coal from another angle, that is, supplying our Canadian needs from

our Canadian mines. We have sufficient coal in Canada to supply all our needs, but unfortunately these coal deposits are so situated geographically that it is somewhat difficult to overcome that handicap and sell our coal in competition with the American products in the markets of central Canada. The most serious problem with regard to unemployment with which we have to contend in Nova Scotia is the industrial centres around the coal producing areas of that province. It is estimated that if we could market an additional two million tons of coal per annum we would be able to take care of the unemployment situation in those centres. According to the returns of the bureau of statistics there are about two million tons of coal used in the manufacturing industries of Ontario over and above the coal supplied by the Nova Scotia mines. There are about nine million tons consumed in Ontario in all, over and above the coal supplied from Nova Scotia and if, with the aid of subventions, we were able to provide the entire coal requirements of Ontario we would be keeping within the country something like $60,000,000 annually.
I believe we could do that with a comparatively small expenditure, probably not more than $5,000,000, and my first submission is that as a national investment we would be furthering our own best interests if we broadened our coal policy in that regard. I believe that would go a long way towards solving our railway problem. It would take up the slack in respect to labour as far as unemployment on our railways is concerned.
Carried.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

I want
to say, Mr. Chairman, that if I am not interrupted I do not intend to take many minutes, but if there is any man in this house who thinks he is going to prevent me from expressing my .opinion by calling "carried," he does not know to whom he is talking.
What I am particularly concerned about to-night is not so much placing my opinions with regard to coal subventions before this committee as it is with regard to a question which was asked here the other evening concerning the possibilities of a trade treaty with Russia. One of tihe items which undoubtedly will be made the subject of discussion in regard to a treaty with Russia will be the matter of coal, and every ton of Russian coal that will come into Canada by virtue of any agreement which may be entered into can have only the effect of displacing a ton

Supply-Miscellaneous-Coal
of Canadian produced coal, which will be bound to lead to increased unemployment in our Canadian mines.
What about anthracite?

Anthracite screenings from Russia will take the place of bituminous coal from the east for power purposes in the manufacturing centres of this country. We Can produce coke in this country to take the place of the very best anthracite in the world. I wish to point out-I have these figures from the fuel board-that last year there was imported into the United States over 400,000 tons of anthracite coal from Russia over a duty of $2 a ton. In my judgment it will be impossible to arrange with Russia, having regard to what they were able to accomplish against a duty of $2 a ton going into the United States, a trade treaty including coal which will not be of serious damage and injury to the coal industry of the Dominion of Canada.
I am of the opinion that many hon. members fail to realize the tremendous economic importance of the coal mines in Nova Scotia. Last year even with the depression there was paid out in wages to the working men of that province over $14,000,000. I say to my friends from Ontario that the industrial centres of Nova Scotia furnish one of the very best markets in Canada for both the manufactured goods and the agricultural products of the great province of Ontario. I propose to develop this feature further if I am spared1 at another session; we of the maritime provinces at confederation were given the assurance that we might expect the market for our coal not alone of Quebec but of Ontario. I can prove that from the records antecedent to confederation. Economically we have a splendid case for the consideration of the government, and from the standpoint of the development of this dominion we in the maritime provinces have a right to expect the most favourable consideration.
I have been associated more or less with public life for the last forty years, and one of the great questions always before the public of the maritime provinces has been the attitude of the federal government in regard to coal and steel. I should like to see in this parliament favourable consideration given to that subject, and as far as I am concerned if I felt that I contributed in the least degree towards a policy which would stabilize the attitude of all governments toward this great industry, to bring it out of the doldrums in which it has been struggling for some time and place it on a basis whereby those who have their money invested in this great enterprise will be able to
go forward and develop it so that it can make the contribution of which it is capable towards the economic life of this dominion, I shall be amply satisfied. I regret that I have taken so much time, but I feel very keenly on this matter. I want to emphasize my profound fear with regard to the question of Russian coal coming into competition with coal produced in Canada.

I had intended to make some extended remarks in connection with the subvention for coal, but briefly I want to protest on behalf of New Brunswick against the fact that the coal miners in that province have not received the same consideration as have the coal operators in Nova Scotia. I am glad indeed that Nova Scotia has received this consideration, but we have a thousand men employed in the town and area of Minto, who for the last four or five years had almost steady employment. But to-day they are working only two or three days a week. The coal operators have applied to the government but have received no consideration, and on that ground I want to register a complaint on their behalf.
Would the minister kindly tell the committee the basis of this subvention to the mining industry of the maritime provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The arrangement was
entered into a little over ten years ago, or rather the subvention principle was adopted. The purpose was to put Canadian coal, particularly that from Nova Scotia, into a position to compete effectively with coal imported from the United States. To do that a complicated system of accounting was worked out. The subventions have been paid since that time on the basis of what is required to enable Nova Scotia coal to compete with American coal.
A rate per ton per mile.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, based on a rate per ton per mile, and undoubtedly it resulted in a great deal of Nova Scotia coal moving to the western part of Quebec and on into a considerable area of Ontario.
Will the minister inform the committee how much coal was involved in this item of $1,950,000? Can he tell the committee how it works out per ton?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I cannot at the moment give the information as to the number of tons that were assisted. The amount paid in subventions last year was slightly under $2,000,000. Some of that went to western Canada; one figure that sticks in my memory is that the subvention paid on the movement
Supply-M iscellaneous-Coal

of Alberta coal into Ontario last year was $65,000. It was at the rate of $2.25 a ton. The information is available; I can give it in a moment.

About
1.400.000	tons for Nova Scotia.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
As the hon. member for Cape Breton North-Victoria has said, the amount of coal which received subvention assistance last year from Nova Scotia amounted to about 1,400,000 tons. To be exact-and I always want to give the exact information to the hon. member-it is
1.498.000	tons.
The minister does give that information, and I do not ask for it very often. It works out to $1.40 a ton.
There is more besides that. What about western Canada coal?
There is very little.
Oh, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The average on the Nova Scotia coal is 83 cents per ton.

Eighty-three cents is not very much, but at the same time I always feel these subventions are not consistent with the Liberal policy. I hope some day we shall get away from coal and wheat subventions. I always like to get at the costs of production between this and other countries with which we compete. I do not wish to delay the passing of the vote, but my view is that the cost of Nova Scotia coal at the mine mouth is probably fifty per cent higher than similar coal in the United States. I do not wish to go into that question now, but it is an important point. When the matter is raised at another session we shall give it further consideration.

The
report of the bureau of statistics shows that bituminous coal from the United States is sold at about $1 a ton higher than Nova Scotia coal is sold at in the markets of Quebec.
I did not hear the hon. member.
The report from the bureau of statistics shows that the average price of bituminous coal from the United States is about $6 a ton in Ontario centres.
I am talking about the cost of coal at the mine mouth.
Well, the cost of coal at the mine mouth, plus railway haul would work out about right.
No; there is no "railway haul" about it; I am talking about coal at the mine mouth.

But you get at it pretty closely by taking the railway haul from the $6 price. May I make one further observation, namely that the production of coal involves about sixty-four per cent labour, a point worthy of consideration.
What is the price of soft coal in Ontario?
I do not know what the retail price is, but I have said that the bureau of statistics has given the total amount paid for it, and it works out to about $6 a ton.
It is $7.50.
I notice a big reduction in the vote. I trust the bonus paid in British Columbia on the coal mined on Vancouver island has not been reduced.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No; I assure the hon. member there is no change.
Has this subvention had the effect of increasing the production of coal in the maritime provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am informed that the production last year was practically the same as in 1934. If we contrast that figure with those of several years ago we find there has been a change. The depression has had its effect. Better methods of using coal for heating purposes, and the use of fuel oil have operated to reduce the normal consumption of ten years ago.
Could the minister give the figures for some years, giving first those for the first year of the subvention, and then those for other years leading up to the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In 1928, with the subvention the production of coal in Nova Scotia amounted to 6,700,000 tons. In 1935 it was
5,800,000	tons.
That is hardly the fair way to put it. The movement to Quebec and Ontario has increased. The increased markets in Ontario and Quebec have been made by the subventions.

I notice we are called upon to vote nearly $2,000,000, and I have observed that since 1928 the vote has been regularly approved. I would gather from the remarks of the minister that at no time including this evening has there been any reservation in so far as labour is con-

Supply Miscellaneous
cerned. I am going to say that where government moneys are concerned there should be a definite reservation that labour should be paid a fair wage in connection with the mining of such coal. I state definitely, positively and from personal knowledge that that has not obtained in the past, in so far as Saskatchewan coal is concerned. In respect of certain agencies there is a premium paid in excess of the cost of mining and placing that coal upon the market in which it is sold. In respect of other agencies there is no relationship between the cost of production and the amount that is paid to labour for the production of such coal. I state, generally, that where government moneys are paid in regard to subventions or subsidies or bonuses, or in respect of tariffs of any kind, the Department of Labour has a distinct and separate responsibility to see to it that labour is cared for and paid the percentage of the cost of production to which it is entitled. In so far as the mining of coal is concerned, in the light of my experience I am going to say definitely and positively that that has not been so in the past.
I beg to endorse emphatically the remarks of the hon. member who has just taken his seat.
Item agreed to.

Does the Prime Minister not think we should adjourn, in view of the fact that the Hansard reporters have been working continuously, and it will be pretty hard to keep at this very much longer. It is now 12.30, Tuesday morning. We could be back at 10.30 a.m., I should think.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If my right hon. friend insists, I will move the adjournment-
Oh, I will not insist.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Possibly we
might run as late as one o'clock, and have it understood that we shall adjourn at that time.

What is the sense in that? It seems to me that we are all tired out and cannot do our work efficiently. As the leader of the opposition has said, I think that more hard-worked than we are are the reporters here. People on the Hansard staff will be forced to work morning, noon and night, with no cessation. It is not fair to carry on in this way.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I remember
a time when frequently this house sat until six o'clock in the morning.
Oh, yes, I have been there, too.
But it did not meet in the morning.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I remember very often when this house sat until six o'clock in the morning towards the concluding part of the session. Certainly, however, the government has no desire to have hon. members or any of the staff unduly taxed at the present time. My impression is that both the staff and hon. members rather hope that we may get through before the king's birthday, and that we were obliging everybody by so doing.
It is the twenty-third now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: However, we might continue I think, until one o'clock.
I do not think that is fair.

Item agreed to.
To provide for report on cultural conditions in Canada (literature, art, drama, education, et cetera, $2,500.

I have no objection, in one sense, to this small item, but I do not like this way of doing things. We had last year an item of this sort, "to provide for a report on cultural conditions in Canada -literature, art, drama, education, et cetera." I understand that this is a sort of disguised grant which is being made for a very laudable purpose, to literary people who need help. I think it is high time that we provided for them in some recognized, regular, decent fashion, and not under a camouflage of this kind. What is the good of carrying this item year after year? Let the grant be made openly and regularly, and in such a way as would approve itself to the people generally.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: This item, I think, was explained to the house a couple of years ago, at the time it first appeared in the estimates. I regarded it as an undertaking which had been made by the previous administration and one, therefore, which should be carried on at least for the present year.
With the approval of the present administration.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My right hon. friend says, "with the approval of the present administration." I think that is quite right. It was a grant to a distinguished literary gentleman in this country and, in the circumstances, seemed to be entirely warranted. But

I agree with my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre, who has just spoken, that it is in the nature of an exceptional grant to an exceptional person, and that in these matters there should perhaps not be so many exceptions.
Is the report made by one person or more than one? In any case where can the reports be found? Are they published or circulated?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is a grant to Sir Charles Roberts. I have no doubt that his report, when it is presented, will be an admirable one.
Is it presented annually to anybody, or is the printed record available?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not think there is any condition about it being an annual report. It no doubt will prove to be a volume of considerable importance.

Item agreed to.
To authorize, subject to the approval of the governor in council, appointment of such extra temporary officers, clerks and employees as may be necessary to carry out the purpose of any of the items in these special supplementary estimates.

What is the amount?
This has been discussed fully. Why is it blank? Is it included in the previous item? There is no amount filled in there. I think something was said about $12,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is a general item
covering the special supplementary estimates in order to permit of the engagement of some temporary help,

Yes, but how much
money is it to be?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No money. It applies
to all of the items in the special supplementary estimates, and' takes the place of a similar provision in the former relief acts with respect to the engagement of temporary assistance for the works contemplated.

But there must be an
amount.
How are they paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Out of the special funds in the various supplementary estimates. I suppose "one dollar" might be put opposite this.

No. It would limit
you. You could not do anything then. We discussed this some evenings ago, and I thought there was some sum mentioned. As it stands now it should be struck out unless 
there is a sum placed there, for the obvious reason that an appropriation which contains no amount is not an appropriation at all. It is not even a blank cheque.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I had that looked into
from the standpoint of legal draftmanship and legal requirements, and I am advised that the language of it is sufficient to make it applicable to any item in these special supplementary estimates, the language being:
To authorize ... the appointment of such extra temporary officers, clerks and employees as may be necessary to carry out the purpose of any of the items in these special supplementary estimates.
It is a proviso with respect to the whole of the items contained in these supplementary estimates, in precisely the same manner as a similar clause in the relief acts of former years made a similar provision with respect to expenditure under them. That is the intention.

I am sure the Prime
Minister will say this is bad. I have heard him so frequently refer to the poor old colonel's authority on Parliamentary Grants. A parliamentary grant that carries with it no sum cannot be said to be an appropriation. Under the relief act, which was a blank cheque, the authority was given to the governor in council to name any sum that might be necessary for that purpose. This is a new proposition, to grant the governor in council unlimited right to make an unlimited expenditure for unlimited purposes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, no.

It is. We may as well
face this frankly and admit it without any question:
To authorize, subject to the approval of the governor in council, appointment of such extra temporary officers, clerks and employees as may be necessary to carry out the purpose of any of the items in these special supplementary estimates.
In other words, if it takes one thousand employees costing a millions dollars, it can be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; that is not the intention, I am sure.
That is what it says. Why not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The intention is to
authorize expenditure for temporary assistance out of each item in these estimates. That is the intention, and I am advised that this section gives the necessary legal authority to do so; that is to say, to provide, for instance, for what we just discussed, let us

Supply-Miscellaneous-Temporary Clerks
say the dry dock improvements at Esquimalt, $8,500. There is authority to take out of that $8,500 as much as may be necessary to pay for the wages of the men on the work. It is not by any means an additional appropriation, but merely provides that the government can take out of each of the appropriations sufficient to pay the men on the work. That is the intention. If there is any doubt about it I shall again check it although I have already done so with the law officers. But that is the fact. Certainly no payments will be made other than out of the individual amounts mentioned in the supplementary estimates and separately voted.
Does the minister mean that these individual votes may be diverted from the specified purposes?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; for the purpose of the item only; positively.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
This is a
proviso proposed by the government which might have been added to several resolutions included in these special supplementary estimates. It has been drafted so as to avoid repetition. It is not unusual to ask that a grant be voted for certain works on condition that they be approved by the governor in council. Vote 419 in these very estimates provides for certain reimbursements to the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railways "upon such terms and conditions as the governor in council may determine." The same proviso is made in vote 420. Vote 425, which is the present one, is nothing but an authorization applicable to several other votes. The fact that it is separate from those votes does not make it irregular. The government has the right to submit to the committee of supply estimates to which conditions are attached. My right hon. friend has referred to Durell's Parliamentary Grants. I will give him, as the authority for what I have said, page 27 of that work.
Yes. That is not this.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Take for example item 314:
To aid, in cooperation with provincial governments concerned, in reestablishment of needy fishermen.
That item of $300,000 has already been granted by parliament for that purpose. Parliament has made the grant and any temporary clerks who are employed in connection with that grant will have to be paid out of the grant. This item does not mean or imply that we are voting any additional money for clerks; the
money has already been voted with respect to the various services which are to be rendered. What this item does is to authorize the appointment of temporary clerks, under authority of the governor in council, where temporary clerks are needed in connection with any of the items for which this parliament has already made appropriations, and to pay them out of those appropriations.

There will be no difficulty about imposing conditions on grants; that is elementary. This item number 425 does not state the essential point to which the Prime Minister has referred, namely, that the amounts will be charged against the appropriations of the several items.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have no objection to it so doing.

I ask the Prime Minister to be fair and look at the item which reads:
To authorize, subject to the approval of the governor in council, appointment of such extra temporary officers, clerks and employees as may be necessary to carry out the purpose of any of the items in these special supplementary estimates.
No mention is made as to what this is to be charged against.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That was the intention.

If that had been there, there would have been no discussion. The right of this house to say that when we appropriate $10,000 for X, that shall include the cost of clerical assistance necessary to put that in operation, is quite within our power. But that has not been said.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is understood.

I suggest the proper way to do this would be to amend the bill which will be based upon these resolutions by inserting a paragraph that any of the items mentioned in the special supplementary estimates shall include the cost of the payment of such extra clerks, and so on as may be necessary for the carrying into effect of the expenditures contemplated by such item.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no objection on the part of the government to such clarification.
This item does not say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The law officers advise that that is the intention.

An intention not expressed is not any good.
