Supply-Miscellaneous-Wheat Board

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My right hon. friend often advises me to take the advice of my legal officers, and until this moment I have done 30. In view of the fact that we shall evidently aot finish to-night, I shall give instructions ihat the words suggested by my right hon. friend be added to this section in order that there may be no doubt whatever that the intention is to charge such costs against the individual votes and not create authority by this item to make further expenditures. This will be considered between now and when the house meets this morning, and the necessary words can be added. I would prefer to amend the item as the bill is already printed.
Item stands.
To provide for payment to the Canadian Wheat Board on account of the liabilities of Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, assumed by the Canadian Wheat Board, under the authority of paragraph (f) of section 7 of the Canadian Wheat Board Act, 1935, $15,856,645.35.
Mr. BENNETT; This item will certainly be opposed as vigorously as it is possible to oppose anything. I consider this is the most monstrous effort I have ever seen to use parliament for a purpose that has not to do with the regular transaction of fair business. Under the agreement given by the crown guaranteeing the ultimate liability or responsibility of the wheat board, it will be determined, when this matter is settled, what is the liability of the crown. But this item is departing entirely from the provisions of the statute. There is no provision for this at all in the wheat board act. In view of the evidence given by Mr. Murray that two-thirds of the sales made were charged against the carry-over, to which this refers, it is quite clear that to pay this money at this time is nothing more or less than an effort to trim up the books in a way that should not be permitted. I put this to the Prime Minister: There is an outstanding guarantee by the Dominion of Canada to pay the ultimate balance that might be due to the banks on the carrying out of the business of the wheat board. The wheat board act provided that the surplus should be taken over by the board. The board took over that surplus from the old cooperative enterprise, and the liability of the old enterprise became the liability of the new wheat board. Mr. Murray said that the sales which were made from time to time were appropriated as to two-thirds against the old balance of wheat taken over from the cooperative enterprise. It is now proposed to fix the value of the wheat that was taken over at the price prevailing on that day, and show a loss of $15,000,000. I just leave it to the Prime Minister and to 
this country whether or not this is even a legitimate exercise of the power conferred upon the government under the wheat board act. I am going to take the trouble to point out the section in order that there may be no misapprehension about it. It is chapter 53 of the statutes of 1935, and paragraph (f) of section 7 reads:
The board shall undertake the marketing of wheat in interprovincial and export trade and for such purposes shall have all the powers of a corporation and without limitation upon such powers the following:-
(f) notwithstanding anything hereinbefore contained, to acquire from Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited, upon terms to be approved by the governor in council, all wheat or contracts to purchase or take delivery of wheat in respect of which the government of Canada has given a guarantee.
The entire number of bushels held by the Canadian cooperative enterprise was transferred to the wheat board under the direction of the government, pursuant to the arrangements made. The banks made the wheat board their debtors instead of the cooperative enterprise. It is now proposed that we should make right, any loss so that a profit may be shown, if possible, for the balance of the transactions. I ask the Prime Minister if that is ordinary business, apart even from anything else. The provision is quite clear that we are assuming the ultimate liability with respect to the transaction. At this moment it is not possible to determine what that loss has been. I think there will be some loss, but that cannot be ascertained until the last bushel of that wheat is sold. Mr. Murray said that two-thirds of the sales made at the date he gave evidence were sales out of the wheat transferred by the cooperative enterprise to the wheat board. How then can the loss be fixed by taking the price it was on that day as against the cost, and showing that as $15,000,000 loss? As a matter of fact, the sales that have been made since may increase or diminish that loss-I assume they will increase it-whereas the sales made from now on to the end of the crop year may diminish the loss. The only time at which this matter can be ultimately decided is at the expiration of the crop year, which is July 31. At that time it can be determined whether or not there is any wheat of the old crop, so to speak, to be carried over as distinguished from the year's crop of 1935. The ultimate loss in the terms of the guarantee can then be established. In fairness to everyone connected with this transaction, I must say that I do not think there is any point in endeavouring to put before us that this loss is more or less than it really is.

Supply-Miscellaneous-Wheat Board

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Hear, hear.
Quite so, and it cannot be determined until the end of the crop year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall deal with that in a moment.
The Minister of Finance can juggle with the figures as much as he likes, but he cannot change that fact.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: When my right hon. friend gives me an opportunity-
Right now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My right hon. friend took the responsibility in his early remarks of accusing me of cooking the books of this government.
I did not say that. I did not use that word at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He said, cooking the books of the country.
I did not say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What did my right hon. friend say?
I did not say that. The minister makes that statement. I deny that I made that statement, and no one heard me say it either.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Will my right hon. friend repeat what he did say?
I say that I made no such statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Will my right hon. friend say he did not use the words "cooking the books"?
I did not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Thank you; that is all I want to know. At any rate, he takes strong exception-
Yes, I certainly do, and I shall talk another day if necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I tell him that this government determined that the people of this country should learn exactly what was the position of this wheat transaction from time to time in the same manner as they would learn if they were shareholders of a corporation which had a similar liability.
This is not a printing mill or a lumber organization.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, we shall look at Hansard.
Yes, we shall look at Hansard.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Canadian Wheat Board Act did not authorize the transfer of the liabilities of the Canadian Wheat Producers-
That is what was done.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -but it did, in its express terms, authorize the board to acquire from the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited, upon terms to be approved by the governor in council, all wheat or contracts to purchase or take delivery of wheat in respect of which the government of Canada had given a guarantee. I assume, perhaps improperly; that those responsible for the language of the statute anticipated a settlement on a definite basis as between wheat producers and the new governmental wheat board which was taking over the wheat. For that reason the price on the day on which the wheat was taken over was taken as the basis of settlement. My right -hon. friend's whole remarks indicate that that involved a process of deception. If he did not mean that he meant nothing.
Mr. Chairman, that is improper language to use. The hon. gentleman complains of the use of words, but that is an improper word to use, and he knows it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My right hon. friend,
then, does not accuse the government in this matter of practising deception.
I did not allege the practice of deception and my hon. friend knows it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are improving right along.
That is another highly improper observation. It will not advance us.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, it won't; "cooking the books" is serious.
If the minister says that I alleged that he cooks the books he makes a statement which is not true.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What was it-doctoring the books?
That is not what I said about the books. I was talking about transactions as shown by this estimate, and the hon. gentleman will find from Hansard what I said.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: I shall deal with that; go on.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My right hon. friend
might have some complaint if, from the time of establishing this $15,000,000 loss, there had subsequently been a profit of which some political use might be made by the government now in office. That is not the case. It is extremely unlikely, nay, all but impossible, that it should be the case. There will be a further loss. I cannot conceive of any circumstances under which a further loss can be avoided. It is merely a question whether or not we should pile up a concealed loss, argue about it, dispute as to what it is, or determine, when we have a definite loss with respect to a a particular year, to take it. If by good fortune that loss should be reduced in a future year, by virtue of something happening which none of us expect can happen with respect to that portion of the wheat, then so much the better. I submit that far from this being unfair to the previous government, or in any way unfair from the standpoint of a business handling of the matter, it is completely the reverse. I want to assure my right hon. friend that it was conceived in that spirit, absolutely in the spirit of getting as nearly as possible a correct assessment of the situation in which the country stood with relation to wheat. I can assure him that as far as I can now see, with respect to the disposal of the wheat prior to the 1935 crop there still will be a further loss for which parliament will have to make provision during the present year.
One o'clock.

The case I have made has been proven by the minister, and I cannot quite understand any man of affairs or business who, reading the statement that the minister made, would desire to pass this estimate. The minister said what is true, that always, in a business, you take your inventories to determine your position, but did you ever hear of doing it at a particular moment because

Supply-Miscellaneous-Wheat Board
you drove out existing men and put somebody else in their places? When is the time to take the inventory? It is at the end of the fiscal year, and why? Because the relief act provided that notwithstanding the provisions of any statute or law the governor in council might, upon terms and conditions which might be agreed upon, enter into agreements and so on, and grant financial assistance to any province and to Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited by way of loan, advance, guarantee or otherwise. And the country did give its guarantee to the wheat producers for the wheat taken over from the cooperative enterprise. Had it been taken over a few days sooner the price would have been higher.
What about the sales that were made a few days later? In the middle of it, just because you got rid of McFarland and Grant, for that reason you fix that as the day and you make the loss from that moment. The time to figure the loss is the time when, by law, every corporation makes its inventory, the end of the fiscal year, which in this case is on the 31st day of July, as every man knows who has any knowledge of business at all. Now the minister tells this committee, "We -took an inventory on the 6th or 7th of December because it pleased us to do so, that being the day on which we fired McFarland and his associates and put in somebody else." That is not the time to take the inventory; the time is the end of the fiscal year, when you take the amount of wheat that has been sold in order to determine the extent of the loss. Suppose wheat had continued at $1, $1.25 or $1.50; what about the inventory then? The date on which the inventory is taken is at the end of the fiscal year.
I repeat that. Look at the accounts of any business; is that not the way in which it is done? How are the assets and liabilities determined? They are determined after inventory, and when is the inventory taken? It is taken at the end of the fiscal year, or on a day that is fixed. That is what is done by everyone for the purposes of the auditors. What do the auditors certify by? By the inventory at the end of the fiscal year. Anyone who knows the elements of business knows that. They do not take an inventory in December for the purpose of making a report on the operations of a company at the end of July. It is no good to say that this is going to give a picture, for it does not give a picture of the facts. It was not a case of putting somebody in charge; it was the continuance of a wheat board, and only the personnel of that board was changed. The liability of the wheat 'board, as provided by law, is under a guarantee given to the banks, and the guarantee to the banks says "ultimate liability." That ultimate liability can be determined only after the end of the sales.
If-and I assume this is what the government intend to do-they think it desirable to say, "on the 31st day of July we had X bushels of wheat, and the loss to this date has been so many millions of dollars," until such time as the wheat has been entirely liquidated, there might be some reason to it, though it is quite certain that the wheat will bring no enhanced price. But whatever price it brings, whether that price increases or decreases the loss is a matter for the determination of the ultimate liability at the expiration of the period of time when the liquidation is complete, whenever that may be. Every man who has had anything to do with business knows that. There is not a balance sheet prepared anywhere in the world on any other basis. What do the auditors certify on? Not on an inventory taken in the middle of the year; but we are asked, because for political reasons you removed three men from the job and put somebody else in, to fix the loss, which you can fix, as the minister said, only when your fiscal year is ended.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not say that.

I am answering that. I think the minister said "once a year"; I am not sure of his exact words, but I think he referred to an annual statement, an annual adjustment of assets and liabilities, and there is not a man who does not know that is the way in which business is transacted. It is because of departures from that principle that disaster usually follows. As far as I am concerned, I say that this is not only unfair-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Unfair to whom?

It is unfair to the enterprise. I am not talking about individuals; it is unfair to the enterprise, because you are taking an inventory, a valuation, on a date other than the day when it should be taken. In the second place you are substituting an immediate determination of liability when the agreement was that this country was to pay only the ultimate liability. You have changed the guarantee, which is based on the ultimate liability. Now this government is asking us to pay on an intermediate liability, a liability that might have been greater or less depending on the date on which the wheat was taken over. If it had been taken over a few days sooner the liability would have been less, but is that the way to determine what
4120	COMMONS
Supply-Miscellaneous-Wheat Board
the real liability is? This can be determined in one way, and in one way only, and that is by the ultimate liquidation of the property, namely the wheat. Then you know what the ultimate liability is. Suppose, although it will not happen-and this is the test to impose -that immediately after the wheat was taken over, it began to enhance in value and by the 31st day of July it reached a figure that Showed not only no loss but a substantial profit. What about the situation then? That is the test. When the wheat is all liquidated the ultimate liability is determined. I put this to the committee: There was a time when, according to the current values of wheat in this country, that transaction showed a substantial profit, in the hands of the cooperative enterprise. That was a real, substantial profit, one measured not by hundreds of thousands of dollars but by millions of dollars.
What date was that?
Along between 1930 and 1935, I think in the early part, when wheat went up to its highest point. I do not carry the months and days in my mind.
What particular year, for instance?

Whatever year it was that wheat went to the high price. It does not matter what the year was; I do not carry in my head the years, months or days, but there was a real profit if you could have sold all the wheat at the price then prevailing.
Hear, hear.
But the way you are doing here, you are acting as though we could have sold all the wheat at the price which prevailed on the 6th of December.
No.
This loss is made up in that way. Let there be no misunderstanding as to how it is made up. This loss is the difference between the arbitrary price fixed on the 6th day of December and the liability.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The value of the wheat on the 6th day of December.
An hon. MEMBER; What year?
The value of the wheat on a fixed date.
But why fix that date when it was not the end of the fiscal year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Because that was the date the board actually took over the wheat.

That is the date on which the liability was assumed by the wheat board.

They did not pay for it; it was provided by another statute that there should be this guarantee. We were especially careful about that very thing, and when the matter was under discussion in this house it was pointed out that what happened was that you had a complete novation by which the liability of the cooperative enterprise was taken over by the wheat board; the guarantee was given by the nation to the wheat board for that liability, against ultimate liability, and ultimate liability means on the realization of the assets.
It is now one o'clock, Mr. Chairman, and I shall complete this argument when we resume.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The minister should have the right to reply.
Of course. I have not finished by any means.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I might call my right hon. friend's attention to the fact that he was sufficiently sure of a loss to pass an order in council agreeing to pay out $8,000,000.
That had nothing to do with that transaction at all. It had not anything to do with this, and the minister knows it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There must have been in my right hon. friend's mind1 an idea at least that that much money could not be realized by the producers for their members. Therefore he was making an effort to reimburse them for something which could not come out of the wheat itself. That involved an assumption of a loss.
No; on the contrary it was a profit, which they did not realize-
Oh, oh.

But anybody knows, if they will apply business principles, that it was a profit which they would have made had they not used their wheat for stabilization. Because it was used for stabilization they said: We must get the money we otherwise would have.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In other words there was a loss of this amount. The wheat is not sold yet. Well, unfortunately it is no use trying to convince my right hon. friend.
My hon. friend certainly will not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I rose with some heat because an accusation-
I made no accusation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I shall not repeat; we shall see what Hansard says. I have no doubt at

Supply-Miscellaneous-Wheat Board
all as to the correctness of the course pursued. The new body created was taking over this wheat from a formerly constituted body. Some basis had to be arranged for the transaction.
And there was; they assumed the liability to the bank. That is what happened. That is all there was about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And between the liability to the bank and the value of the wheat on the day they took it over, there was a difference of S15,800,000.
Certainly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Now, is that clear? My right hon. friend might have some complaint if between then and now, or at any time in the future there was any prospect at all that it would appear that some abnormally low point was taken for some ulterior purpose.
The moment you concede that your case is gone.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not agree that my case is gone.
As a matter of logic it is.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am in the judgment of members of this committee and I shall be in the judgment of future sessions of this parliament with respect to the matter. I have advised the people of Canada, advice which they had never previously received, that as of a certain date they had a loss in connection with this transaction-
They once had a profit.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I admit at once that if the new Wheat Board Act had provided otherwise than it did with respect to the 1936 crop then we would have had to follow a different course, but with respect to the new crop the Wheat Board Act is quite clear, that if a profit is made the farmers are entitled to it through the medium of participation certificates, but a profit on that one crop only, not with respect to the previous crops which formed part of the wheat taken over by the wheat producers.
That is quite clear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Quite clear and quite true. In the meantime further disposal is taking place of the crops prior to that of 1935. There is no doubt at all that further losses will result; my right hon. friend knows it. I desire to show the losses as nearly as possible in the year in which they occur, and to charge them to that year in the accounts of the country. By my right hon. friend's method we would never be admitting a loss until heaven 12739-262
knows when, and then we would have to tell the country it had lost a great deal more than we now state, and provide for it now. In some one fiscal year-

That is exactly the
opposite of what I said.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -instead of having the loss spread with some approximation over the years to which it applies. My right hon. friend has been lecturing me on my lack of wisdom and business judgment and that sort of thing. I have as much right to my opinion as to what constitutes good business as he has, and I think he would have been wiser had he made an approximation of the loss year by year as the years proceeded from 1930 to 1935.
When? In the middle of the year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If he had turned over the wheat to another organization I would expect those responsible for the conduct of that other organization to insist on some valuation with respect to the property they were taking over. I would not like to try to sell to my right hon. friend the kind of pig in a poke which he suggests the ne<w board should have taken over from the old Canadian wheat producers. I would not have a chance in the world.
On the contrary, Mr. Murray said that he would apply the sales on the basis of two-thirds and one-third.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Exactly; he had to have some basis.
Precisely.
One o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Can we not pass this item?

No, not by a long way.
Progress reported.

Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance) moved:
That the resolutions passed this day be now read a second time and concurred in.
Motion agreed to.
